On motion of Sir George Foster (Minister of Trade and Commerce), the House proceeded to consider amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 112, to amend the Canada Grain Act.

The Bill, which was sent up from the House to the Senate and which has been returned with these amendments, was very carefully thought out and thoroughly discussed in the House, and it was sent to the Senate as it had been thought out and as the consensus of opinion in the committee and in the House after it was discussed seemed to dictate. The Senate, however, has fallen foul of one of the sections and has altered it by striking out the word " shippers." This amendment was moved in the House, but it did not seem to receive the assent of the House and was not even pressed to a vote. It, however, has been revived in the Senate and is now part of the Bill as the Senate has returned it to the Commons. It destroys the full efficiency of the Bill and will hamper the work of the department to the extent that this interest is left out of the poivers that are to be given by this legislation to the Grain Commission. At this late time, however, I suppose it is better to take a mutilated Bill than to have no-

thing at all, and with the determination to work it out as well as we can under what has been sent back to us from the Senate,
I propose to let the matter go. I move that the amendments be concurred in.
Amendments concurred in.

The House again in Committee, Mr. Sevigny in the Chair, on Bill No. Ill, to enable Canadians on active military service during the present war to exercise their electoral franchise.-Mr. Doherty.
On section 4, subsection 6-holding polls:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
When this subsection
was allowed to stand, it was after certain suggestions, had been made with regard to making some matters that might be considered to be covered by it perfectly clear, one of them being that the volunteer presenting himself at the poll to vote should be subject to being called upon *o be sworn then and there. A second thing that was pointed out was that while subsection 6 does provide by reference to the Dominion Elections Act for agents, or what are called scrutineers, to be present at the polls, in view of the circumstances in which the votes will be taken and of the fact that they may be taken for more than one electoral district, it is desirable to provide that agents may be present at the polls as agents, not necessarily exclusively of any one candidate, but of all candidates of the party for which they are appointed scrutineers.
Finally, it was suggested that it would be wise that we should put in a provision to require the military authorities of the different camps to give all possible facilities for the holding of the polls. To meet these three suggestions, I have prepared amendments. I move that subsection 6 of section 4 be amended by adding thereto:
" 6a. Any volunteer presenting' himself to vote shall, if so required, even though his name be upon the list prepared by the camp returning officer, take the oath contained in form B of this Act and in form Y of the Dominion Elections Act, and if his claim to vote rests upon his having been a qualified elector in any electoral district at the time of his enlistment or appointment, any other oath which under the Dominion Elections Act may be required to be taken by voters generally claiming a like qualification.
" 6b. In addition to agents who may be appointed in accordance with the Dominion Elections Act to represent candidates at the poll, agents may be appointed on behalf of either the Government or the Opposition and such agents shall have all the powers of agents of candidates under the said Act and be entitled
to exercise the said powers on behalf of all candidates in all electoral districts for the party by which such agents have been named and any person or persons named as agent or agents of any candidate of a party shall be entitled to act as agent or agents of any other candidate of the same party in any electoral district or districts.	-
"*6c. The military authorities at every camp or base where a poll is to be held as aforesaid shall afford to the camp returning officer all necessary facilities for the holding of the same."
The effect will be to make it quite clear that the volunteer may be sworn both according to form B and according to form Y, the latter being against disqualification or any corrupt act on his part or exercised upon him, and also any further oath under the Dominion Elections Act which may be required of those claiming like qualification.

Last night I understood
the minister to say that he would propose an amendment that would make it absolutely clear that the voter had a right to vote although his name was not on the list prepared by the returning officer. Has that been done? Is it the intention to make that provision?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have no objection to it now, but it seemed to me that, inasmuch as there is absolutely nothing here to make the presence of the name on the lists that the returning officer provides an essential condition of voting, what the hon. gentleman desires would necessarily follow. I confess I overlooked the matter in preparing the amendments, but I have no objection to providing it. I move:
That subsection 4 of section 4 be amended by adding thereto the words:
" The failure of the volunteer to present his claim in time to be entered on such list, and the consequent absence of his name from such list, shall not deprive such volunteer of his right to vote, provided he presents himself to the returning officer and takes the oath above prescribed before the poll is closed."
Will the words, "oath above prescribed," preclude the possibility of his being required to take the qualification and bribery oath?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think so. This , provides that the mere absence of his name from the list shall not preclude his voting, provided he takes the oath entitling him to get on the list. That being dealt with, I think he fairly comes under the provisions of subsection 6, which requires him to present himself to the returning officer and make before the returning officer an affi-

davit which will entitle him to get on the list. The words, " any volunteer presenting himself to vote," will apply to that man when he presents himself to vote just as it will apply to the man whose name was on the list.
So long as there is no confusion, I am perfectly satisfied.

With regard to the amendment proposed by the minister respecting the furnishing of facilities by the camp commandant to the returning officer of the poll, the minister will remember that last night I suggested that a provision should be inserted requiring the camp commandant to give all volunteers in camp an opportunity to poll their votes. I pointed out the difficulty that might arise if a man were employed at some work which might prevent him from voting. Perhaps the minister could add some apt words which would make provision for this.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I did not understand
that the desire was that we should impose an obligation on them to allow the men to vote, because I take it that it is not desirable that we should require the military authorities to allow a man to absent himself from essential duties for the purpose of voting. However, I would have no objection to meeting the hon. gentleman's view.
We are dealing only with Canadian camps in this case, and I see no reason, unless it be confinement for some offence, why every man in the camp should not be permitted to vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I understand that the
desire would be met if we added to subsection 6c the following words:
And the officer commanding shall allow every volunteer, so far as it may he done consistently with the proper performance of his military duties, time and opportunity to vote.
Amendments agreed to.

On schedule B-affidavit:

There are numerous cases where these men come from outside an electoral district in which they enlisted, and perhaps in the electoral district only three or four days or a week before enlistment. That precludes their taking the oath that they have been thirty days there. How would that affect them?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As the Bill now reads a man is entitled to vote in the electoral district in which he last resided for a period of thirty days within the six months previous to his enlistment.
No, it is the thirty days preceding.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, we have cleared away any question of its being immediately preceding.

The words in the affidavit are: ''the last place in which I was resident for thirty days." Does not that point out to the voter that he must have resided thirty days in one place immediately prior to his enlistment?
That is the way I read it.
It seems to me that that is the way it has to be interpreted.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, if a man states the last place within which he has lived for thirty days during the last six months, he does not say anything about it being the thirty days immediately preceding his enlistment. It may be that within six months a certain place is the only place in 'which he had resided for thirty days, and he may have resided there four months ago. I do not quite see why it is inferred that because a man has to say where, during the last six months, he last lived for thirty days it means the last place in which he has lived for a shorter period.
He must give the particular place in which he lived for thirty days within the six months?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

I want to call the minister's attention to the fact that there are a number of Canadian officers who have taken commissions in British regular regiments. Most of them are surplus officers who went over with the first contingent. From New Brunswick we have five such officers. I understand that there are 75 or 80 officers, or non-commissioned officers, who have taken commissions. It would be desirable to give these men a chance to vote and it might be done by inserting a provision in the Bill that Canadian officers with temporary commissions in the regular service may apply to the High Commissioner for affidavits and ballots, and, upon their being marked, may send the affidavits and ballots to the High Commissioner to be forwarded by him. It would give them an opportunity to vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is unfortunate that these individual gentlemen should lose their opportunity to vote, but on the Other hand I think we are doing our full duty when we endeavour to provide for the members of the Canadian expeditionary force. To go outside and select a few people who have gone into the regular British army, and are not connected with the Canadian force, and try to provide a further method for their voting, is endeavouring to get a degree of perfection that will expose us to possible complications that the results would hardly justify. There, are officers who are Canadians in some of the forces of the Allied armies, and it would be difficult for us to make the same provision for them. Upon the whole, I think that, having made a provision that seems adequately to cover the Canadian expeditionary force, it will probably be wiser for us not to endeavour to extend it further.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What does my hon. friend suggest?

Each officer, whether a commanding officer, a captain, or a sergeant, will have a certain number of men in his unit, who are to vote, and my suggestion is that notice should be given that on such a day and at such a place he will proceed to receive these votes. Otherwise, a man could come in and vote one day, another man to-morrow, another man the next day, and so on. What I had in mind was that notice should be given to those who are entitled to vote before such an officer, that on such a day and at such a place he would receive their votes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It would be very difficult to collect them all at the one place and on the same day.
I do not deny that it is difficult, but it is only one of the difficulties surrounding this measure.

There would be no difficulty on that score in Canada, or in Bermuda, or in England. If the vote is to be allowed at all in France or in Belgium, I am sure the commanding officers could arrange to have some one representing the parties present. All that we on this side of

the House want is that the vote coming from the firing line should be an honest vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I desire to point out
that when mention was made of my having refused yesterday to allow notice to be given, we were discussing a plan of official scrutineers, and what I was unwilling to undertake was that it should be an obligation of the officer taking the votes to see that the scrutineers were notified. It seems to me that if that system could be worked out, it would be more proper to require diligence on the part of the scrutineer to attend on the officer than to lay an obligation on the officer to run after the scrutineer. In order to meet a view in which I concurred, that is, that so far as possible we shall provide for observation of the operation of taking the votes, I desire to move:
That subsection 4 of section 2 be reconsidered -for the purpose of adding thereto the following words:
" In cases where conditions make it possible, the officer empowered to receive affidavits and votes shall give notice of the time and place where he will receive such affidavits and votes, and shall permit any one officer, non commissioner officer or soldier who may desire to do so, to be present at said operations and act as agent of the respective parties, Government and Opposition, and any independent candidate, in the same manner as agents of candidates are empowered to act at a poll under the Dominion Elections Act. No volunteer who is entitled to vote and prevented by his military duties from voting at such time and place shall, however, be precluded from so doing at same other time and place."
I think, as we have allowed for the possibility of a voter voting for an independent candidate, it might be well to allow repre-. sentation of such possible independent candidate.
Amendment agreed to.

According to the wording in the beginning of section 4, a returning officer is to be appointed at each military camp or base. At Edmonton there are two regiments of infantry occupying military buildings. In the case of the squadron, which is on the south side of the river, its base is at Medicine Hat; but it has the use of the armoury at Edmonton, and the men are billeted amongst the citizens. Would this be considered as a camp, and would this force have a returning officer under the interpretation of this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would feel that it ought to be treated as such. To remove

all doubt I have no objection to putting in a section that shall interpret the word " camp."
If the word " base " were not used, the word " camp " would cover everything, but when the word base is used and when the men are not at their base and not at their"camp there is confusion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There are conditions under which soldiers would not be in a camp. But we can interpret the word " camp." We struck out section 10. I move that the following be enacted as section 10 of the Bill:	.
" In this Act the word ' camp ' shall include any barrack or barracks or other place where ahy unit or units are assembled for the purpose of military duties under a commanding officer."
Amendment agreed to.

May 1 ask if there has been any change in the title of the Bill? In this corrected reprint it is entitled, " An Act to enable Canadians on active military service during tihe present war to exercise their electoral franchise." But the Bill as it now stands enables others than Canadians to exercise their electoral franchise-for instance, persons in the British islands or other overseas Dominions who come within section 1.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They must form part of the Canadian military forces.
But it says " to enable Canadians."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Tlhey are persons enlisted in Canada.
Yes, but they are not Canadians. I think the title should be amended to meet the provisions of the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Suppose we said " Canadian soldiers." I think that would describe them correctly. Whatever they may be as to nationality, when they join the Canadian permanent force or the Canadian expeditionary force, they are certainly correctly described as Canadian soldiers.
Would it not be more correct to say "to enable persons serving in the military service of Canada " ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
A better wording, perhaps, would be, " to enable persons serving in the Canadian military forces." But I may remind my hon. friend that the title is dealt with on the third reading.
Bill as amended reported.
Mr. DOHERTY moved the third reading of the Bill.

I move in amendment:
That this Bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole House, with instructions that they have power to amend the same by striking out section 2 and inserting in lieu thereof the following:
" The Governor in Council shall appoint two commissioners for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of this Act, one of whom shall be nominated toy the Prime Minister and one by the leader of the Opposition, within ten days after the passing hereof. And on failure of either the Prime Minister or the leader of tne Opposition to make such nomination, the Governor in Council may make the appointment of the commissioner which either of such parties so failed to nominate. The said commissioners so appointed shall appoint a third commissioner within ten days of their being notified by the Governor in Council of their appointment, and should they fail to agree on such third commissioner, such third commissioner shall on the request of either or both of the said two commissioners be appointed by the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada. In case of the death, resignation or refusal to act at any time of either of such commissioners his place shall be filled in manner hereinbefore prescribed for the appointment of the said commissioner who so died, resigned or refused to act. The majority of the commissioners shall constitute a quorum and their acts shall be as legal and valid as the joint acts of the three commissioners.
" The said commissioners shall have power and it shall toe their duty from time to time* to make all necessary regulations for the taking of the votes, the marking of the ballots, the taking of the affidavits of the voters and the transmission thereof to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery and all procedure in connection therewith, so as to insure as far as possible that all persons entitled to vote hereunder shall have a fair and reasonable opportunity of doing so. Such regulation shall be subject to the approval of the Governor in Council. And when they have been so approved they shall have the same force and effect as if they were enacted as a part of this Act.
" The commissioners shall have power to appoint such persons to act as scrutineers and otherwise to assist in carrying out the said regulations as the commissioners may deem necessary from time to time."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The matter
which the hon. gentleman has just brought to the attention of the House was debated very fully in committee, and reply was made by the hon. Minister of Justice to the arguments put forward in support of that suggestion. It is neither necessary nor desirable that these arguments should be repeated, and I hope that the hon. gentleman will not consider it discourteous if at this juncture we do not repeat them.

The matter was fully
discussed in committee; I did not intend that we should go into it now.
Amendment (Mr. Pugsley) negatived on division.

I desire to move, seconded by Mr. Lemieux:
That this Bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the Committee ot the Whole House with instructions that they have power to amend the same by adding as subsection 11 of section 2 the following:
" 11. No action shall be taken under the foregoing provisions of this section until the same have been submitted to and approved by the Secretary for War of the United Kingdom."
This matter was discussed fully in committee, in the absence of the Prime Minister, and I do not propose now to add anything in support of this amendment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: As the hon. gentleman has already moved one amendment, he has exhausted his right to speak on the third reading. The amendment which he now proposes is, therefore, out of order.

I beg to move this
amendment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
This matter
also was fully discussed in committee, and it is not necessary nor desirable that we should add anything to the arguments which were made by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice in that respect. The only observation I desire to make is that the amendment as proposed, if carried into effect, would seem to constitute a very severe blow at the autonomy of Canada and the independence of this Parliament.

I do not take the view which my right hon. friend takes, for this reason: this Bill imposes certain duties upon officers of the British Army. It is made imperative upon these officers that they shall deliver ballots to Canadian soldiers who are entitled to use them; that they shall take their affidavits; that they shall place the different ballots and affidavits in envelopes; that they shall seal these envelopes and forward them in packages to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. That is imposing duties upon Imperial officers over whom this Government and this Parliament have no control whatever. It would seem to me, therefore, that before any action should be taken in the way of attempting to have these officers assume the functions which are- specified in the Bill and take upon themselves the obligations which, by the Bill, they are required

to take, it is only reasonable that the consent of the Secretary of State for War, who has jurisdiction and control over all these officers, should first be obtained. I cannot see how that would in any way derogate from the dignity, authority or autonomy of this Parliament.
Amendment (Mr. Lemieux) negatived on division.

I beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for Sunbury and Queens (Mr. H. II. McLean):
That this Bill be not read a third time, but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole House, with instructions that they have power to amend the same by striking out the words " twenty-one " in the first line of section one and by inserting the word " eighteen " in place thereof.
The House has already heard the arguments in support of this suggestion. I contend very respectfully that a man who has attained 18 years of age, who has undergone medical inspection, who is mentally and physically qualified to take up arms in the service of his country overseas, and who is willing to make the sacrifice of his life, if necessary, to defend the cause which he has at heart, should be on an equal footing with men of the age of 21. If the soldier who has attained the age of 21 years is to have the advantage of exercising the franchise, then it is an unjust and unfortunate discrimination that others who are serving their country should be deprived of that right. I think that this view will appeal to the whole of young Canada, which is taking a deep and patriotic interest in this matter.
Amendment (Mr. Marcil) negatived on division.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I beg to move that the title of the Bill be as follows: An Act to enable Canadian Soldiers on Active Military Service During the Present War to Exercise their Electoral Franchise.

Motion agreed to.
Main motion (Mr. Doherty) agreed to, and Bill read the third time and passed
At one o'clock, the House took recess.
The House resumed at three o'clock.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a report was made by the Public Accounts Committee yesterday and the House has not yet concurred in that report. It was in-

tended to have made the usual motion for concurrence this morning, but I asked that it might be postponed, as I desired to make a statement in respect of it, having regard to the fact that the report or reports concerned contain some matter that demands the serious consideration of the Government. .It would be possible to allow it to stand until to-morrow morning; but I would suggest, if the House has no objection, that the motion be taken at eight o'clock this evening for the purpose of having it disposed of and for the further purpose of giving me an opportunity to make the statement to which I have alluded. I would therefore move, if the House will consent, that motions shall be taken at eight o'clock this evening.
Motion agreed to.

I wish to ask a question of the Postmaster General. I have here one of the new war-tax stamps for cheques, notes, etc., and I see it is exactly similar to the ordinary postage stamp, with the words " Canada postage " printed on it in the usual way, but with the words " war tax " on it. Is this special war tax stamp good for the payment of postage on a letter in the ordinary way? I was told in one of the banks this morning' that a number of letters were returned to them yesterday- that the boys had, by inadvertence, placed the stamps marked war tax on them and that they were refused at the central post office. I understand that the ordinary postage stamp is good for payment of the special war tax. Is it also true that the war stamp is good for ordinary postage? If not, great confusion may result owing to the close resemblance between the two stamps.

I am not prepared to
make a statement yet, but if the hon. gentleman will allow the question to stand until eight o'clock I shall reply fully. My impression is that the war-tax stamp is not available for the ordinary postage of letters.

Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Edmonton) asked for leave to move the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing a matter of urgent public importance, namely, the report of Mr. T. R. Ferguson regarding the Department of the Interior.
And leave having been granted, he said: 1601
Mr. Speaker, there have been laid upon the table of the House within the past few days certain reports made by one T. R. Ferguson, who was appointed a commissioner by Order in Council, which has also been placed on the table. In order that the House may be aware of the scope of the inquiry, it may perhaps be as well to read, in whole or in part, the orders under which Mr. .Ferguson worked. There are two. The first of these is dated the 10th of May, 1913, passed under the Inquiries Act of 1906, and appoints Mr. Ferguson a commissioner.
-to investigate and report upon all matters connected with the sale, lease, grant, exchange or disposition by any means whatsoever, since the 1st day of July, 1896, of (a) Dominion lands, (b) timber and mineral lands and mining rights and privileges, including coal, petroleum and gas lands and rights; (c) water-powers and rights, under the authority or purporting to be under authority of the Dominion Lands Act, Irrigation Act, or other statutes of the Parliament of Canada.
It will be observed that this gives Mr. Ferguson a fairly comprehensive range of activity, but it did not seem to be considered adequate for the purposes in view; and so, on the 27th of June, 1913, the order was amended to provide that Mr. Ferguson be appointed a commissioner under Part I of the Inquiries Act:
To investigate and report upon all matters relating to or connected with the application for (although such application may not have been granted or may be still pending), the sale, lease, grant, exchange or disposition by any means whatsoever, since the 1st day of July, 1896 of (a) Dominion lands; (b) timber and mineral lands and mining rights and privileges, including coal, petroleum and gas lands and rights and irrigation tracts or lands; and the cutting of timber upon Government lands; (c) water-powers and rights;	(d) Indian lands
and Indian reserves.
In pursuance of this authority, Mr. Ferguson entered upon his duties, and that he was more or less diligent in the performance of those duties may fairly be gathered from the reports showing the results of his efforts, which have been laid upon the table of the House in the past few days and are now before the House for their inspection and consideration. I may say, for information, that I understand that Mr. Ferguson's services were enlisted at a codt of approximately $30,000 in the way of salary and $10,000 for expenses. This report thus represents an outlay of approximately $40,000. So there is no question that Mr. Ferguson had an ample range of authority, and there is no doubt that he had plenty of financial backing; nor is there any doubt that he has volumes of documents to show

as the result of his activities. It would be ignoring the plain facts not to admit or take for granted that the purpose of Mr. Ferguson's appointment was to find actions that would be blameworthy on the part of myself as Minister of the Interior or on the part of my predecessor in that office. That, I take it, was the sole and only purpose of the appointment of Mr. Ferguson. No other reason, I think, can fairly he adduced.
As a result of this exhaustive examination that he has made, this unlimited investigation that he to as been authorized to make, and that the country has paid for, certainly with unlimited liberality, I think I am safe in saying that both the Administration of my predecessor and that of myself have received at the hands of Mr. Ferguson what may be considered a very satisfactory certificate of character. There can he no doubt of the fact that Mr. Ferguson's investigations were prompted by political animus rather than by a sincere desire to secure the protection of the public interest. There have been many transactions of the Interior Department since 1896, but of all these thousands of transactions, we find by these reports that Mr. Ferguson has only dealt with the transactions that in some way are linked with the name of some person who is either a prominent Liberal in public life or a prominent official appointed by the Liberal Government. If Mr. Ferguson has not made any successful discoveries it certainly is not for want of authority, or for want of political animus. Besides that, it may be noted that while the second order that was issued to empower Mr. Ferguson to extend his inquiries was issued to enable 'him to take cognizance of unfinished transactions, and transactions entered upon by the Government of the day, there is no reference to any such transactions in any of these documents. Mr. Ferguson has confined himself almost entirely to transactions which already have been aired on the floor of Parliament, and to which, I am bound to say, his investigations toave added very little in the way of information to the public.
While I do not wish to introduce a controversial attitude in the discussion of , this report, I think it is only due to the country that it should be informed that this report, which obviously has been in large measure [DOT]completed for a very long time, and I fancy has been entirely completed for a considerable time, was not presented to Parliament at a period of the session that would permit of a full and fair examination and
IMr. Oliver.]
discussion by Parliament or of such scrutiny as such an extensive and voluminous report would naturally be entitled to. It will be observed that while this report deals with matters concerning the operations of the Interior Department, no part of it was laid on the table of the House until the Estimates of the Department of the Interior and, may I say as well, the Estimates of the Department of Public Works had passed the House. Immediately those Estimates had passed, the volumes containing the report of the investigations began to be laid on the table. It is obvious that the animus on the part of the commissioner was behind the commissioner as well. It was not the intention of the Government that appointed that commission that the results of its work should be considered in Parliament fairly and impartially or that the questions arising under it Should be discussed in Parliament as they should have been discussed and as they could only or best be discussed in Committee of the Whole House during the discussion of the Estimates of the department.
I have already said that there is no fault to find with the majority of the conclusions reached by Mr. Ferguson; but although there is not, these documents have been laid on the table of Parliament at a time when they do not admit of a reasonable measure of examination or discussion or consideration, but at a time when the public press has every opportunity to obtain knowledge of these documents and to place any construction it pleases upon any part of the matter contained. The Government laid itself out in the beginning to take all the advantage that lay in its hands, by reason of having control of the affairs of the country, and' by reason of the Act providing for investigations in regard to public matters, and over, above and beyond that, they further took the strategical, practical, political, partisan and picayune advantage of bringing these documents before Parliament at a time when they cannot be properly considered or discussed, and at a time when all the political capital that can possibly be made out of them can be made out of them by the newspaper friends of our hon. friends on the other side of the House. I have no fault to find with the appointment of a commissioner to investigate the transactions of the Interior Department under my Administration or anybody else's administration. The transactions of the Interior Department are the business of the public, and the public have a right to be informed in

regard to those transactions. They have a right, especially, if there is any suspicion, and I have no doubt there was suspicion in the minds of our hon. friends opposite as to the character of the transactions involved. Therefore, I say that the Government had a perfect right to appoint a commissioner to make all the investigation that is possible or that they think is necessary. But they have no right, having done that, having invoked the extreme power of the law in protection of the public interest, to turn that to a petty, partisan advantage as they have done in the case of this report.
Now, dealing with the different separate reports, I will first take the one with which my name is particularly connected. I have here the report upon the matter, and it is described as:
He the Bulletin Company, Limited, the Honourable Frank Oliver, and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company.
Not to weary the House by going into any very great detail, I may say that the subject-matter of this report is the statement that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company hold $15,000 of stock in the Bulletin Company, Limited, in which company I also hold a large amount of stock, or thj controlling interest; that is, the controlling interest is in my name. The Grand Trunk Pacific Company, some time about 1905 or 1906, took shares in that company to the amount of $15,000. I do not know that it is of interest either to the House or to the country what the financial operations of the Bulletin Company, Limited, may be; but on that point I may mention that the Bulletin newspaper was founded , by me, became a limited liability company later, and was conducted upon lines suitable to the circumstances of the city and surrounding country up to the point when the great development began as a result of the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway and the extension of the Canadian Northern railway. About that time, I transferred my activities to Ottawa, in an endeavour to help along the interests of the country in the administration of the Interior Department, and naturally I left the Bulletin to take care of itself. If the newspaper was to continue its development in proportion to the changed circumstances of the country, it became necessary that it should have increased capital. A new company was formed, to which some of the leading citizens of Edmonton subscribed money, and to which it appears from the record , that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company subscribed $15,000. I took shares for the interest I had in the company, and the business has gone on in that way ever since.
I do not know whether it would be of interest to the House and the country to know that the business has not been prosperous, and in all probability the Grand Trunk Pacific Company have lost their $15,000, as I have lost a good many thousand dollars also as a result of my connection with the Bulletin Company, Limited.
I only allude to this because it is alluded to in this document.
I find further, on considering this document, that Mr. Ferguson apparently had in his mind the idea that the Grand Trunk Pacfie Company had bought $15,000 . worth of influence in the administration of the Interior Department, by taking this amount of stock in the Bulletin Company.
I say that his purpose was to discover whether or not the Grand Trunk Pacific Company had bought $15,000 worth of influence in the Interior Department by taking this stock in the Bulletin Company, Limited; but after having made an exhaustive investigation, Mr. Ferguson does not find that. He did not find that the company had any influence in the administration of the Interior Department or he would have said so. He carefully does not say so, and what he says is:
With regard to the propriety of the transaction as detailed herein, I do not know that it is necessary for me to comment upon the same at any length.
Now, after the evidence of animus that is shown throughout the transaction connected with the operations of Mr. Ferguson, after the investigation that he made as shown by his report, to find if the Grand Trunk Pacific had received advantage because of the ownership of stock in the Bulletin Company,, after all his efforts he has not been able to find anything upon which he can hang: even the suggestion of that influence, because if he had he would have said so. It. was in order to enable him to say so that this country has paid between $36,000 and $40,000 for this report that is now lying before us. Mr. Ferguson says:
Although I endeavoured to obtain some explanation from the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company as to why it should, and did, go into this transaction, I have been unable to do so.
And he continues:
As the evidence reveals in purchasing the stock the company was doing something which

was quite out of its usual line of business, and contrary to the custom of the company. That it was not regarded as of the nature of an investment would appear from the fact that the company, from the day of the purchase of tihe stock until the present *time, has paid no attention to the affairs or management of the Bulletin Company, or attended any of its meetings. and no dividends have ever been received.
It was a mystery to Mr. Ferguson why the Grand Trunk Pacific Company desired to take stock in the Bulletin Company; I suppose it was just as much a mystery to him why a number of gentlemen in the city of Edmonton took stock in the Bulletin Company. But it was no mystery to anybody who knows the circumstances of the case. These men desired to see the newspaper expanded to correspond with the new conditions of the city, and I presume that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, being interested in Edmonton, as a junction and terminal point, felt a like interest and were willing to take stock for that purpose. But it makes no difference what the purpose of the G-rand Trunk Pacific .Company was, the result which Mr. Ferguson wished to find has been achieved or not achieved, and that is the only thing in which, as I understand it, the House and the country is concerned. It is too bad that Mr. Ferguson was disappointed to the extent he was; it is too bad that our friends on the other side of the House have not been able to get what they expected for their expenditure of the money of the country, but there is the report, and that is the only conclusion that can be drawn from it.
There is, however, something else that may be brought to the attention of the House in connection with this report, and it is this- I wish all members of the House to realize just what has been done in this case. The Government of Canada, in partisan pursuit of a political opponent, took the authority that is vested in them for the purpose of furthering the public interest, in order to establish an inquisitorial inquiry into the piivate business of a political opponent, as to a matter with which the Government of Canada had no more business to deal than it has to deal with the private business of any other political opponent.
I will admit that if Mr. Ferguson had found any evidence of improper collusion between myself as Minister of the Interior and the Grand Trunk Pacific, then he would have been warranted in inquiring as to what relationship existed between us; but that was not where he started apparently. He started to inquire into the private business of the Bulletin Company,

Limited, as on the same principle he could start an inquiry into the private business of any private individual in this Dominion and expose that private business to the public gaze at the will, wish, suggestion or whim of the Government of the day. In my humble opinion, this is a most dangerous precedent and an action which will not find approval at the hands of the people of Canada. Power is vested in the hands of the Government for the purpose of protecting the public interest and not for the purpose of carrying on partisan warfare by methods which are generally relegated to porch-climbers or thugs. When the Government of Canada descends to that sort of political action, it disgraces Canada as well as itself. I do not fear any result that can be achieved by any Government of this country which chooses to make its fight supposedly in the public interest on any such principle, because, as is well-known by the members of this House, I have been the subject of blackmailing attacks for the past several years, and I do not think that those attacks have either done me any harm or done those who instigated them any good; and in so far as this attack, which is of the same character, goes, I think the result will be identical. When the Government of the day directs such an engine against a member of the Opposition, turning the authority of the Government into a means of political blackmail, it is establishing itself in a position of authority amongst even its own followers, and I think even its own followers will question the desirability of its existence. Supposing one of our hon. friends on the other side does not see eye to eye with the Government of the day on some important question, it is possible for the Government to appoint a commission of inquiry that will go into that man's private affairs, which may or may not be just as able to stand the light of day as the affairs of the Bulletin Company, Ltd., and to compel a loyalty of support on the part of its own followers that it is not entitled to receive and would not receive by reason of any other consideration. This principle of introducing blackmail into politics is a dangerous principle, and it is just as dangerous to supporters of the Government as it is to members of the Opposition.
I wish next to deal with the reference to my colleague, Mr. Cruise, the hon. member for Dauphin. Mr. Cruise moved for this report on the 15th of March; and although there is no doubt at all that the report was prepared at that time and had been prepared

months before, it was not brought down until after Mr. Cruise, believing that the business of the House was practically finished, had gone home, so that he is not here to answer for himself in regard to this report; but, as it contains some reflections upon Mr. Cruise and indirectly upon myself, I propose to have a word or two to say in regard to it. Broadly speaking, I may say that the accusation is that Mr. Cruise acquired a homestead on misrepresentation and without having fulfilled the duties, and that this occurred through the improper and lax administration of the officials of the Department of the Interior for which, of course,
I was responsible. This accusation has gone out through the press to all parts of the country, this being the intention of Mr. Ferguson when he made his report and the intention of the Government when they held it until Mr. Cruise was absent and when they laid it on the table of the House at the time they did lay it.
What happened was this:	The Riding
Mountain Forest reserve had been set apart some years before by Order in Council or by departmental order, I do not know which. Owing to the fact that the reservation had not been carefully examined before being made, some parts of the area included were suitable for settlement, and squatters went on these parts. When by the Act of 1906, these reservations were made by statute, and a more careful examination was made of the forest conditions existing within them, a new line was drawn which excluded some quarters and included others in the reserve. It became necessary for the Government to take action to rid the reserve of those squatters who were inside of the boundaries, and to dispose under equitable conditions of the lands which had hitherto been reserved, but which were now excluded, and upon which there were some squatters. A Mr. Davis, who had been a forest ranger, was appointed to attend to this work, which of necessity must be handled on the ground and by personal examination. It was a difficult piece of work to do; we had to get rid of the squatters who remained on the permanent reserve, and we got rid of them by compensating them-by giving them other land largely in the area that was permanently cut out of the reserve. In dealing, then, with the lands that were out ol the reserve, we gave precedence to the men who were in occupation as squatters, and then disposed of the remaining lands to applicants as they came forward. For some considerable period before the Government took the action that I have
stated, there had been a movement on to these reserves. Some men went on and established permanent improvemerits and went into residence; some established temporary improvements and did not go into residence. liVhen we were disposing of the land that had been taken out of the reserve, we considered claims as to priority oi right of selection, so that it was necessary that a man should have actually resided or squatted upon the land while it was still in the reserve. If there were tangible, substantial improvements, we recognized that the owner of them had a prior right over somebody who -had not improved. That was the position of Mr. Cruise. He is an old homesteader in the Dauphin district. He was entitled to a second homestead. . Having hopes, as others had, that this area would be cut out of the Riding Mountain reserve, in order to establish a priority right, I presume, he caused the beginning of a building to the erected in 1906, while the land was still on the reserve. Then, when the land was cut out of the reserve, he applied for homestead rights upon this land, and was accorded these rights on the ground that he had improvements on the land prior to that time. Mr. Ferguson suggests that Mr. Cruise acquired these rights by fraud or misrepresentation. There is absolutely no warrant whatever for that statement.
Now, as to Mr. Cruise securing patent. He entered under the provision of proving up by the ranging of cattle upon the land. His permanent residence was within nine miles of the locality, so he did not need to be in actual residence in order to prove up. All he needed was twenty head of cattle upon that land. He had-so this evidence goes to show-only thirteen head of cattle of his own at that time. He bought seven head from a neighbour and gave a promissory note in payment; and on the strength of the ownership of these twenty cattle, he acquired patent for this land-absolutely, unquestionably in accordance with the letter of the law as -it stood at that time. Mr. Ferguson does not think so. He thinks that Mr. Cruise did not get his patent according to the law. I say that that is a misrepresentation on the part of Mr. Ferguson. And it is neither more nor less than an outrage on the part of this Government, that after having such a report in their hands, and it having been asked for by the member affected by it, they did not bring it forward when they

had it there, and give him a chance on the floor of this House to state his actual position in regard to it. I may say that the use of cattls for the purpose of proving up the right of homestead was subject to abuse, and there were cases in which, while the letter of the law was fulfilled, the spirit was not fulfilled. And because of that, in 1908, an amendment was made in the law abolishing the right to prove up by ranging cattle on the homestead. This Government that appointed Mr. Ferguson and finds fault with Mr. Cruise for having proved up with cattle, absolutely within the terms of the law, has reinstated that provision so that anybody can prove up a homestead anywhere in the West exactly as Mr. Cruise proved up this homestead-can do it to-day. Mr. Ferguson concludes his report as follows:
There does not appear to he a proper or adequate supervision of the grants for sale of public lands. If as suggested in other reports there had been a supervisor appointed who was reponsible for the legal and proper grant of each quarter-section granted, the frauds above mentioned could not have been perpetrated.	-
Mr. Davis was appointed as supervisor and had personal supervision and responsibility over and for these transactions. Mr. Ferguson uses the word "fraud" with a view to creating the impression that the country was in some way defrauded by the action of Mr. Davis. There was no fraud upon the country, in any way, shape or manner. The lands were there available for homestead, and the only question that is raised in the evidence offered by Mr. Ferguson is whether Mr. Davis gave due consideration to the rights of priority in the application made to these lands. It was a question between one applicant and another, and not between the applicants on one side and the country or the Government on the other. Mr. Ferguson has deliberately undertaken to create a false impression in regard to this case which has been taken advantage of by the newspapers supporting hon. gentlemen opposite. And I take the liberty of repeating that such a course is not politics, it is not partisanship, it is simply plain ordinary po lit cal brigandage.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
I am afraid the hon. member is a little extravagant. I would remind him that it is not in order to impute an improper motive in what is done by an individual member of Parliament or by a number of members of Parliament collectively. Being an old member of the House, I naturally expect the hon. member 
not to be guilty of an infraction of the rules.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: Is it the same company?

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
Yes, the Southern Alberta Land Company. The amount was voted last year, and revoted again this year.
I think it would be only losing time to read all that Mr. Ferguson has written in the conclusion of his report, but the final conclusion that he reaches, is this:
After discussion of the matter with several experts of the United States of America, where irrigation has been very extensively carried on, that the proper method is that irrigation should be carried on under government supervision and control.
That may be very true, but the Government had not adopted the principle of government supervision at that time. The policy of the Government was to use the value of the land as a means of securing its development by irrigation, 4 p.m. and in pursuance of that policy this arrangement with the Southern Alberta Land Company was entered into. As I say, it is being carried out by the company to the satisfaction of this Government, to the extent that they are willing to pay $140,000 to the company in assistance of their enterprise. I presume, however, that in all these pages Mr. Ferguson is desirous of creating the
impression that the company should not have got the land. I presume, further, that his effort was to prove that in my administration of the department I had done some wrong to the country in allowing the company to spend their money by the million in that effort.
Here is another irrigation proposition: the Aylwin Company, E. A. Robert and J. D. McGregor. This report is even bulkier than the former one, and I have not been able to go through it in its entirety. I have only a very indistinct recollection of this transaction, but as near as I can follow Mr. Ferguson's idea, while he desires to create the impression that the late Government acted unwisely and unjustly in giving the land to the Southern Alberta Company, ihe finds fault with the late Government for not having given the land to the Aylwin Company, because a large part of it was opened to homestead entry. That is as much as I can make out of his report. Apparently a man named Aylwin applied for an irrigation tract, making certain representations to the department as to his ability to put water on the land. Later it was found that he could not put water on the land-either the water was not there, or (he could not get it-and as a consequence his right lapsed and part of the tract was opened up to homestead entry, and was actually homesteaded. Part of it was under grazing lease, and, I fancy, in consideration of whatever steps the Aylwin Company had taken, they were confirmed in their rights in so far as the grazing lease was concerned. They afterwards entered into a transaction witih the Southern Alberta Land Company, and the Southern Alberta Land Company acquired the whole tract. Upon it, as I say, they have spent large sums of money, and of that enterprise the Government has substantially approved.
Mr. Ferguson reaches the sage conclusion :	,
X conclude by saying that this seems to have been really a granting of this particular tract. to individual promoters, who looked for enrichment. That they did not make very large sums out of it, is no fault of theirs. If these applicants had been informed that the Government policy was such that they bind themselves to irrigate, that they would not be allowed to sell or dispose of their interests, that they must irrigate and begin the work and carry it on themselves, it is altogether likely they would never have endeavoured to acquire this tract. In such an event-in this case at any rate

these purchasers would not have acquired it, as they would necessarily have taken the trouble to learn, and have learned, that the tract could not be irrigated.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: When was the land expropriated ?

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
I think about 1910.
I find here a " report on a grazing ranch J. G. Turriff, A. J. Adamson and J. D. McGregor." This transaction was ventilated in the House of Commons a number of years ago. I do not think anything new is added in this report to what was said in the House at that time. I take it that Mr. Ferguson makes this report simply for the purpose of bringing into undesirable prominence the name of my friend and colleague, the, member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), and for no other

reason that can be conceived. The transaction relates to a grazing lease, application for which was made by one Brown. The application was made at a time when closed grazing leases were allowed; that is, they were closed for 21 years. In some way Brown's application did not go through. After I became minister, I cancelled Ithe regulations providing for closed leases for 21 years and provided that all 21-year closed leases should be cancellable on two years' notice. The applicants pressed for the granting of their lease. I decided that as we were trying "to clear off the conditions that had existed up to that time in regard to closed leases, and as we were trying to establish new conditions,' it was desirable that we should do so having regard to the rights already existing. I granted, as the evidence will show, a closed lease to the people who were the assigns of Brown. I do not know whether it was in the name of these gentlemen or not, but we will assume that it was. These men became the beneficial owners of Brown's application under the action I took, under the principles I laid down and the principles upon which I acted. We were making a very sudden and radical change in grazing regulations. We had to get the acceptance and approval of the people of the West to that change, and in order to get that acceptance it was desirable to clear off all existing or vested rights. I have no doubt that if we had taken the action that, has been taken by our friends on the other side of the House in dealing with some of their political opponents, we would have said to every man whose lease had not been closed up: There is nothing doing; you are through. We did not do that, and I do not think it is good policy on the part of our friends opposite to do it; however, that is their business. We have granted this as a closed lease because application had been made for it, and the conditions in a certain measure had been fulfilled and the law was that closed leases could be had. Mr. Ferguson says that we did not charge the $2,400 rental that we should have charged these parties. That may be true, but on the other hand, the parties had not had the beneficial use of the lease during that time. There may have been an undue leniency in regard to the $2,400, and on the other hand there may not have been. I do not know that this Government is absolutely justified in taking $2,400 out of a private individual unless that private individual has had reasonable value for the money. Since it
is a question that was in dispute, since it was awaiting adjudication, and since it needed further consideration, I am not prepared to admit that we should have charged that rental, although I am quite prepared to admit that we could have done so if we had seen fit. Mr. Ferguson's conclusion is:
All of which goes to show the necessity for great care and attention in the carrying out not only departmental detail, but in guarding against errors and misunderstanding of those unfamiliar with the file, justifying' my suggestions in other reports relative to the appointment of a supervisor of the different steps taken in different matters in the department.
That is his conclusion in regard to wihat has been heralded through the country by the press supporting our friends on the other side of the House as a most iniquitous transaction.
I find here a report on timber berths, with the names of W. H. Nolan, A. W. Fraser, K.C., and J. G. Turriff. I do not recall that this was under my administration, and I will leave this report for my hon. friend (Mr. Turriff) to deal with.
Here are two cases: The Kananaskis Coal Company, Limited, with the names of Howard Douglas, George E. Hunter and Walter Carret and others, and timber berths 550-558. As far as I have been able to gather from a glance through these reports, there is no suggestion that these people got anything that they did not pay for. The suggestion is, that being ofiicers of the Government, they had no right, and they should not have been permitted to deal in Government property. With that contention I have no fault to find, and in so far as my administration was concerned, certainly I did not permit ofiicers of the department to have transactions in the property of the Government. But it is only fair to these parties to point out that the business of the Department of the Interior increased in magnitude and value very rapidly from year to year during the period immediately before I became minister and while I was minister. Dealing with these questions from the point of view of the conditions as they prevailed in 1911, it is not fair to consider them from the point of view of the conditions that prevailed in 1900 or 1896. What was of little value in 1896 became three, four, five, six or ten times as valuable in 1911. From time to time it became necessary in the administration of the affairs of the Department of the Interior to make a change to meet the new conditions. What was

quite permissible in years before ceased to be permissible as values and interests increased. When these men acquired these properties, in so far as I can say, they acquired them either by themselves or by assignment from other people who had acquired them in the ordinary way, and it has yet to be shown that the public interest suffered in any degree.
The first charge is that the men themselves should not have dealt with Government property. With that conclusion I have no fault to find, and as far as my knowledge went no member of the department did deal in Government property while I was minister. The connection of these men with the department had ceased, the connection of some of them having ceased before I was minister, and if there is any justice in the matter, justice has been done and there was no necessity in the wide world in the public interest of dragging these men's names, in an undesirable connection, before the Parliament and people of Canada, or of spending the money of the people in going over cases that were already settled and in regard to which the commissioner makes no suggestion as to any other action to be taken.
I find a report here: " re the Blood Indian Reserve and Frank Pedley." Frank Pedley was Deputy Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs, and as nearly as I can gather from what I see here, about 1903, before I became minister, a lease of the grazing rights on the Blood Indian Reserve was granted to one McEwan, of Brandon. McEwan afterwards took into his interest in the grazing lease Peter Ryan of Toronto, and Gordon, Ironsides, and Fares, of Winnipeg. There is no question about the propriety of the lease. These people agreed to pay $5,000 a year for the grazing rights; they paid the money, and it was a sound business transaction from start to finish so far as I understand it. Gordon, Ironsides and Fares, were great cattlemen; they needed the grazing lands; the Indians were not using them; and it was good business to lease'the grazing rights in these reserves to somebody who would use the lands and give the Indians the financial benefits of that use. That was the transaction, and that was what was done.
There is no question about the responsibility of the parties concerned; there is no question as to the fact that they paid a fair price for what they got; but this whole report is an attempt to prove that Frank Pedley had some financial interest in the
[Mr. Oliver.!
transaction. Frank Pedley is not in the department to-day; he has nothing whatever to do with the affairs of this country, and there was no sound reason in the world for Mr. Ferguson spending his time on this report, or no sound reason in the world for laying this report on the table of Parliament, except the partisan reason to make ' party politics pending a general election that the Government is ashamed to announce they are going to hold. Pedley's connection with this, so he informs me, was this:	Peter Ryan, one of the lessees
of this reserve owed Pedley money, or he owed the Bank of Commerce money upon Pedley's endorsation; that is, Pedley had endorsed Ryan's paper in the Bank of Commerce, and this occurred before there was any lease at all. Later on the Bank of Commerce pressed for payment and Ryan assigned a part of his interest in the lease to one Bedford Jones. Jones sold the interest to one Miller for $1,000, and the money was applied to reduce Ryan's indebtedness to the Bank of Commerce. And for that reason Mr. Pedley's name must be dragged through the columns of the Conservative press in this country, in terms that would certainly not be more than justified if Mr. Pedley were a horse-thief instead of a respectable citizen, who did good service to this country as Deputy Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs, and who has no reason not to look any man in the eye, let it be the Prime Minister, of Canada or Mr. T. R. Ferguson.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: Does the report show that Mr. Pedley got nothing out of it?

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: I have been trying to tell my hon. friend that.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: Does it show that he only got a thousand dollars?

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: He admits that he got more.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
I have stated what I have been able to gather from this report. This shows the unfairness of putting these reports upon the table at this time of the session, and I hope I shall not be declared out of order when I say that if my hon. friends opposite choose to take that course they must take the logical consequence of it, which is, that they have taken an undue and partisan advantage which is not to their credit nor to the benefit of good government in this country. It is not . right that an attempt should be made to use the vast authority of the Government of

Canada to pillory any honest citizen before the people of this country.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: Do I understand the hon. member to say that the $1,000 was used to reduce Mr. Ryan's indebtedness to Mr. Pedley?

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: I said it was used to reduce his indebtedness to the Bank of Commerce.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: Then my hon. friend has not read the report.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
Perhaps I have not read
it as carefully as the Solicitor General has, but if he had an opportunity to read it, would it not have been decent to place it on the table and let the rest of us have an opportunity to read it?

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: There will be no hurry; we can stay here a week if the hon. gentleman wishes.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
I thank the Solicitor General for the suggestion, and it is/a fair sample of the kind of politics that is being played by gentlemen on the other side of the House. We have closed up the business of the session, we have transacted all the business the Government has offered us, we have voted the Supplies, we have passed all the legislation, and now the Solicitor General throws upon the table a pile of documents which apparently he has carefully studied, and he says:	If ybu want a fair
discussion on this, all you have to do is to prolong the session, with no other business before Parliament than the discussion of this subject. The Solicitor General can campaign the country during the coming general election on that policy, and I do not think he will get very far with it.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: Is the hon. member aware that Mr. Pedley was examined before Mr. Ferguson some time ago?

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: And the hon. gentleman learned from Mr. Pedley the result of the inquiry?

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: And so the hon. gentleman is not surprised to-day?	.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: I am not surprised to-day; but I have not had time to read the report. I have merely been able to give Mr. Pedley's side of the story.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
knows, then, what is alleged against
Mr. Pedley as related by Mr. Pedley himself, and that took place some months ago. Do I understand from the hon. gentleman that Mr. Pedley did not acquaint him with the investigation?

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: Then, if the hon. gentleman never heard from Mr. Pedley anything about it, he is taken by surprise to-day.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
Mr. Ferguson's report with regard to Mr. Pedley came down here two or three days ago, and I happened to meet Mr. Pedley, and I asked him about it. I had not read the report; I had not seen it. He gave me what I have given to the House, and I am prepared to take his word in regard to that quite as much as that of Mr. Ferguson, or any other hired thug such as he is.
I find another report here on " Indian lands; re James A. Smart, Frank Pedley, and William J. White." Of course the major part of the transactions alluded to in this report took place before I was minister, and again I say I have not had an opportunity of considering them very carefully. As I gather, the allegation is that Smart, Pedley and White-Smart being Deputy Minister of the Interior, and Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, Pedley being Superintendent of Immigration, and White being a subordinate officer in the Immigration Department-formed a company of some kind to acquire Indian lands. Now, I have already said that on the question of the interference of officers of the Government in the property of the people I do not suggest for a moment justification for that action. I have pointed out that as conditions changed, what was permissible at one time became unpermitted at another time, and, whatever occurred, two of these gentlemen are out of the service of the Government to-day; one of them was out of it before I became minister at all, and he was the only one who had anything to do with the Indian Department and the third man is still in the service of the Government.
As far as I have been able to follow the report, there is no suggestion that these men in purchasing Indian lands got an acre of them for less than its full value; they paid dollar for dollar for everything that they got. That being the case, the Indian got what was coming to him; the country is discharged of its obligation to the Indian inasmuch as he got all that was coming to him, and the only question at issue is the

propriety of Government officials meddling with public property. In regard to that matter, there is nothing in the report to indicate that it happened while I was minister. I certainly object to it, and I would not allow officers of the department, to my knowledge, to take such action. They must take their choice and speculate outside of the department, or refrain from speculating inside the department. That being the fact, however, there was no warrant for Mr. Ferguson spending the money of this country in securing evidence to this extent for the purpose of proving what every one will admit and bringing a report before Parliament in regard to one man who has not been in the Government service for, I think, over ten years, in regard to another man with whose services our friends on the other side have seen fit to dispense, and in regard to the third man who still is in the Government employ. Either Mr. Ferguson was anxious to put in his time in the preparation of this report-and I think he got $50 for every working day-or he was not able to find anything very serious in the way of delinquency in the Department of the Interior. If he could have found something more serious, than the mere fact that these gentlemen bought Indian lands, by tender, taking their chances, getting them if their tender was the highest and not getting them if their tender was not. Mr. Ferguson was not using his time to good advantage when he spent so much of it in order to get this report, and I take it as a certificate of character to the administration of the department, to myself and to my. predecessor that Mr. Ferguson,	in	all	his search
of two years at $50	a day, with
all the authority of the Government behind him, with all the political animus that naturally went with himself and with those .that put him into the position, was not able to do better than he did for his employers. Therefore we can take it for granted that under the Liberal Administration the people of Canada had an Administration of their Interior and Indian Affairs that was entirely and highly to their credit and to their benefit.
For a man who is paid $50 a day to find fault, over whom there is no control in any way, shape or form, who can say what he likes, and who Iby getting individuals into a solitary room and threatening them with process of law, is entitled to take down whatever he can compel them to say and to produce it before Parliament, it is possible to make a very much worse story than he has been able to make, so that if

the results have been as they have been under the Liberal Administration, the country is still to be congratulated on the Administration it has received. It is an old saying that the proof of the pudding is in the eating, and we can judge best of Administration by results. As regards the values of land, when the Liberal Administration came into office, the railway companies and the Hudson Bay Company, that had the sale of lands in the Northwest, sold 108,000 acres at an average price of $3.34 per acre. This was all picked land, and they all wanted to sell and most of them employed special selling agents, but the best they could get for 108,000 acres of picked land was only $3.34 an acre. It took some time of Liberal Administration, of administration in the interests of the people of Canada, before the confidence of the people was inspired in the country so that the land advanced in price, because in 1900 the average price was only $3.27; in 1901, $3.36; in 1902, $3.56; in 1903, $3.46; but from 1903, with the inception of the railway policy of the Liberal Administration, the land of the West immediately began to increase in price, and it was $4.39 in 1904; $5.09 in 1905; $6.01 in 1906; $6.02 in 1907; $8.80 in 1908; $11.08 in 1909; $13.36 in 1910 and $13.59 in 1911. In that year the companies sold 1,406,651 acres at $13.59 an acre, the largest sale that had ever been made in any year or that has ever been made since. It is true that in 1914 the average price increased to $14.75, but the quantity of safes decreased to 501,575 acres; that is to say, the price of land increased by a little over a dollar an acre, 'but the sales decreased by over 900,000 acres. If the Administration of the Interior Department needed the advice that Mr. Ferguson has so kindly given it in all these reports, if it were so lax and slack and if so much fraud were perpetrated, it is not reasonable to suppose that the people would have had confidence in the country so that they would have rushed upon it and taken up homesteads in continually increasing numbers each year under the Liberal Administration, but this is What they did. In 1902, there were 14,673 entries; in 1903, 31,383; in 1904, 26,073; in 1905, 30,819; in 1906, 41,869; for the nine months of 1907 when there was the change in the fiscal year, 21,647; in 1908, 30,424; in 1909, 39,081; in 1910, 41,568, and in 1911,	44,479, or practically 44,500.
But as soon as our friends got in and waved the magic wand of " leave well enough alone", entries began to drop, and in 1912 we had 39,000; in 1913; 33,000; 1914, 31,000. And they are still going down.

So I say that while the country must be grateful to Mr. Ferguson for the advice he has given as to the administration of the Interior Department, we think that this advice, if it is worth anything, if it is worth the money this country has paid for it, had better be tendered to our friends on the other side, and they had better take advantage of it, because the country absolutely needs some change in its administration from what it is getting at the present time, as compared with what it got under the late Administration.
As I said in the beginning, here is a report that has cost the country isomething in the neighbourhood of forty thousand dollars, which must be accepted as absolute evidence that under Liberal Administration our lands in all departments were administered as honestly as they were efficiently, and as the country's record shows they were efficiently administered.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. J. ROCHE (Minister of the Interior) :
speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
The hon. member for Edmonton
(Mr. Oliver) has shown a good deal of heat because the Government has seen fit to appoint Mr. Ferguson as commissioner to inquire into the matters relating to the Interior Department over which the hon. gentleman formerly presided. I do not think he should find so much fault with the Government in investigating certain matters which had more or less a relation to his own administration of the department. I do not think he has very much reason to find fault because of the late time when, as he says, this report has been submitted. The report only came into my possession late in the month of March. It is true, I desired to peruse it before laying it upon the table. The session was in progress, and for the greater part of the time there have been three sittings a day. I had only time to hastily peruse the report and it was' submitted to the House at the earliest possible moment under the circumstances. I think he is toierably familiar with most of the matters discussed here to-day by reason of the fact that he was at the head of the department at the time they occurred, although I agree with him that after a lapse of time one's memory cannot be expected to retain all the details of these various transactions.
