speechtext:
I am very sorry that I
was too flattering.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
We certainly have some
idea of the hon. gentleman's capacity for using adjectives of a most pronounced character. We are quite willing to award him the palm, because for any one on this side of the House to try to rival him would simply be vain.
In view of the taunts flung across the floor of the House from time to time, I have simply thought it my duty to bring these matters up, although Mr. Ferguson did not deal with them. Had he been given a little longer time, I have no doubt that some of the matters to which I have just referred would have been investigated by him, but I think I have made sufficient investigation as to what is in the files to warrant me in making every statement

that I have made to-night. I do not wish to be strong in my language, no matter how great the temptation may be. I have not dealt with this question from a personal standpoint, because I have no personal feeling in regard to the matter. Were I to allow my personal feelings to weigh with me, I would say nothing whatever about these matters; but, being in charge of the department that has been under criticism by hon. members opposite during this session, especially by the ex-Minister of the Interior, I would be expected to do my duty, especially when he is simulating such righteous indignation against what has been exposed in the committees, in showing the character of the Administration which was carried on while he was Minister of the Interior and while the Liberal Government was in power. I think I have disclosed sufficient in the few minutes that I have spent in addressing the House this evening to show that the people of this country did not get rid of the late Government any too soon. The late Government has frittered away the public domain, scattering it out amongst its own political friends. In the light of such events, it ill-becomes hon. gentlemen opposite to attempt to criticise, as they have criticised in this House, the administration either of the Department of the Interior or of any other department of this Government.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
I have to say at once that I do not rise for the purpose of discussing the matters which have been brought to the attention of the House by my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), followed by my hon. friend the present Minister of the Interior. I must confess my ignorance of the matters under discussion. On Monday morning, on looking over the Votes and Proceedings of the previous Saturday, I found that the Secretary of State had laid two returns on the table of the House. The record in the Votes and Proceedings reads as follows:
Mr. Coderre presented,-Return to an Order of the House, of the 22nd February, 1915, for a copy of the report of investigation held about June 1, 1914, by T. R. Ferguson, as special commissioner, into the allotment of homesteads on the area cut out of the Riding Mountain Forest Reserve in the year 1908 or about that time.
Mr. Coderre laid on the Table of the House, -Report of Thomas R. Ferguson, commissioner appointed to investigate matters pertaining to the Blood Indian Reserve and the acquisition of certain Indian lands by Messrs. James A. Smart, Frank Pedley and William J. White, together with the evidence taken in the said investigation.

I sent at once to the clerk of the House for these reports, and he sent me, not the whole of the report which is now upon the table, but the report concerning the Blood Indian reserve. Looking at it, I found that the reference upon which Mr. Ferguson had acted was not to be found in the paper, and the following day I asked for it and it was laid on the table yesterday. I commenced to read the report; but I am sorry to say that I have not gone veiy far, for I have perused only some 2G or 25 pages. I had not the remotest suspicion at that moment that I would find my name mentioned in this report, nor had I any notice of it until I saw an article in the Ottawa Citizen of this date under the rather glaring headlines:
Western land deal with local end is laid bare-F. P. and H. A. Aylwin and J. A. Robert of Ottawa figure in irrigation case with big profits-negotiation through Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier.
I think it better, for the information of the House and the people and for all concerned, myself in particular, that I should read to the House the whole of this article, which is as follows:
A further report by T. R. Ferguson, K.C., brought down in the Commons this morning, deals with the Aylwin irrigation tract. The application, the report states, was made by F. P. Aylwin, of Ottawa, and the acreage was 69,000. The comm'sdoner finds that E. A. Robert, of Montreal, was largely instrumental in obtaining the grant and that he benefited from it. J. Alfred Robert, of Ottawa, was another beneficiary. The report finds that Mr. E. A. Robert's services were enlisted for a consideration, and that he was paid $12,420 in that connection. The transaction took place in 1909. The land was located 75 miles west of Medicine Hat and in connection with the transaction the report finds that the Messrs. Robert and three others got $18,461 each. The commissioner states that it was not feasible to irrigate the tract.
Mr. Ferguson, dealing with the facts of the case, notes that it was necessary to procure the services of Mr. Robert. The application was made by Cam'lle Pich6, of Montreal, who was then a member of Parliament, and there were five partners: C. H. Newton, of Winnipeg, H. P. Simpson, of Vancouver, F. P. and H. A. Aylwin, of Ottawa, and J. A. Robert, of Ottawa. It was stated that the condition on which E. A. Robert became connected wTiih the case was that his brother should have a fifth interest and he should be paid 18 cents an acre for every acre granted.
The commissioner states that according to the Order in Council $500,000 was mentioned as the cost of the scheme when it was proposed to grant 311,000 acres, and he adds that it was to cost the same amount when 69,000 acres were granted. If the tract could be irrigated he does not see why it was granted and goes on to state that some steps should be taken to prevent speculators acquiring irriga-

tion tracts and making profits by turning them over. This case he refers to as one destined to benefit individual promoters looking for enrichment.
The total amount received by Mr. Robert and his associates was $270,100 which, after providing for expenses and certain amounts paid to associates, left a profit of $92,329.
The commissioner is unable to find that the grant of this land was in the public interest. No great benefit could result to the public from the irrigation of 17,000 acres which was called for in the contract.
A letter is quoted under date of June 19, 1908, wherein Mr. Robert wrote that he had seen the " chief " and had a long talk with him on the matter. . Mr. Robert expressed fears that others might try to get in over his head and he says he got the assurance that if he and his friends did not get in, no others would.
On June 19, 1908, Mr. Robert wrote to H. A. Aylwin in respect to certain other parties wno he feared might get the grant. He expressed the opinion that they would not get it, but that he and his associates would and, if so, they would be dealt with " on terms acceptable to ourselves."
On March 18, 1908, Mr. Robert again wrote Mr. Aylwin to the effect that he understood Mr. Oliver had thrown open the tract to homesteaders. He added that other than being evident that Oliver had not been straight in the matter he would not let it worry him as the matter was in such shape that the grant had to be made or one of a similar size given. "I am going up to see Sir Wilfrid in a day or so," he added, "and perhaps shall have some good news to send you on my return. Keep your friends quiet until you hear from me and I am as certain as ever that you will get your grant of land. The delay has been very annoying and disgusting, but they are in a worse position to refuse it to-day than they were some time ago."
The commissioner observes that Mr. Robert's deals were not with the minister of the department, but with Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Hon. R.' Leiraieux, and that twelve days after the 18th March, the minister took up for the second time consideration of Aylwin's application.
On August 14, 1908, Mr. Robert advised H. A. Aylwin that there was no further need to worry over it, that before many days there would be word that would be satisfactory.
Mr. Ferguson adds that the grant should not have been made until there was a complete investigation to see if the scheme was feasible. No engineers' reports were asked for and the conclusion he comes to is that the " insistent requests of Mr. Robert were the real reason for the grant."
The land was later transferred to the Alberta Land Company, organized by Mr. Robert.
That is the whole of the article. Now I come back to the headlines:
F. P. and H. A. Aylwin and J. A. Robert, of Ottawa, figure In irrigation case with big profits-Negotiations through Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
As to these Messrs. Aylwin, I do not think I know either one or the other. With Mr. J. A. Robert I may have a slight 162
acquaintance. If I ever met him, it was not more than once in my life. Mr. E. A. Robert I know very well, have known him for many years, and have always counted him a friend. The gist of the charges in this paper is the following sentence:
Commissioner observes) that Mr. Robert's deals were not with the minister of the department, but with Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Hon. R. Lem eux, and that twelve days after the 18th March, the minister took up for the second time consideration of Aylwin's application.
There is an inference there, as stated in the headlines, that the negotiations with regard to these lands were through Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I have simply this to say -that to this statement there is not a shadow of truth. Whether the lease was right or whether it was wrong, constitutionally I am responsible, and I do not intend to deny the responsibility which attaches to me, as I was then of the Government. But personally I know nothing of this matter, and if I dealt with it at all-of which I have no recollection at the present time-it was simply departmentally in the absence of the minister. Mr. Robert speaks in one of these letters as having come to me and seen me. Mr. Robert may have seen me; if he says so, he did see me. This article says:
A letter is quoted under daite of June 19, 1908, wherein Mr Robert wrote that he had seen the " chief " and had a long talk with him on the matter. Mr. Robert expressed fears that others might try to get in over his head, and he says that he got the assurance that if he and his friends did not get it, no others would.
I have no exception to take to that; I may have said to Mr. Robert that if he did not get it nobody else would, as he was the first applicant. Of all this I have not at the moment the slightest recollection. Will it surprise the House, will it surprise the Government, most of all will it surprise the Prime Minister, if I say that it is impossible for me, after six or eight years, to remember a private' conversation which may have taken place in my office when I was Prime Minister? Everybody will know that the Prime Minister sees in his office ten, twenty, forty, fifty persons every day, coming with their grievances, some of consequence and some of no consequence; some to whom he will give attention and some to whom he will give no attention. It is a matter of daily occurrence for some one to come to the Prime Minister complaining that he has not had satisfaction from one of his



ministers; and it is also a matter of everyday occurrence, and a matter of common knowledge, that sometimes the Prime Minister deems it his bounden duty to interfere, but in most cases he does not interfere.
Now/ in all fairness, if Mr. Ferguson had wanted to create the impression that I was in any way responsible

personally and not merely constitutionally responsible-that I had anything to do with tlhe transaction right .or wrong, I ask, in the name of fair play, in the name of common honesty, why did not he call me as a witness? I put myself in the judgment of hon. members on the other side as well as of those on this side. I have been for a great many years in public life, and up to this time I have escaped, I think, scandal. Have I not a right, then, if an accusation is to be bandied against me in the public prints, and on the floor of this House, upon the report of a commissioner, to say that at least this man should have -given me the fair play of an opportunity of stating my version of the case? How can I be expected to give any information upon this subject? But I am satisfied of one thing-I have not had time to look at the evidence; my attention was called to this matter only two hours ago; but I should be very much surprised if Mr. Robert ever stated that I was an intermediary in connection with these negotiations. The evidence has Been examined by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, and, if they can find in it anything to that effect, I invite them to bring it to my attention. I have tried to find in the report evidence to justify the assertion that I was an intermediary in this matter; I find no statement, but some insinuations. I think I ought to read the conclusion of Mr. Ferguson's report; it is as follows:
So far as Mr. P. P. Aylwin, the nominal applicant was concerned, he was not considered. Mr. Robert was the active man. Again I say; if this tract could not be irrigated, why was it granted? It seems unaccountable, unless one concedes that it was to satisfy the requests of Mr. E. A. Robert and his associates. The claims made from time to time by him in his letters to his associates, in which he insists frequently that he will secure the tract; his actions in buying out the interests of Charles H. Newton, and assuming a liability of $23,600 and agreeing to pay $5,000 as a bonus after the tract had been thrown open to homesteading, all goes to show that he, at least, was satisfied that departmental action was of no importance- that in the end he would get the tract. He was not, it is true, aware of all that was going on in the department. At the earlier stages of the application, at any rate, he believed that there would be granted something over 300,000 acres, and apparently he did not for months learn of

the practical cancellation of the tract. After he had learned of it, he persisted, and the small tract was granted. Even then he did not know that the irrigation privileges and rights no lpnger accompanied the grant, although they were a most material portion of the grant. Nevertheless, undeniably it was the efforts of Mr. E. A. Robert which procured the grant of the tract.
After a consideration of the grant of this irrigation tract, and of the tract of the Southern Alberta Land Company, I am of the opinion that there should be a change in the department in connection with the granting of the irrigation traots. As is mentioned in my report relative to the Southern Alberta Land Company, I consider that irrigation tracts should not be granted to private individuals or to corporations, but that such irrigation schemes should be undertaken by the Government for the benefit of the country at large. If such a course is not followed, then there should be some regulation governing the amount of acreage to be granted, and providing also that no tract should under any circumstances be granted until the fullest and completest details as to the feasibility of -the scheme are placed before the department and the department is satisfied that the scheme can and will be fully carried on to completion. Some course should be followed to prevent speculators acquiring tracts and making large profits by turning them over. All such profits form a charge upon the lands which the settler must ultimately pay, and certainly cannot be in the interests of the public at large. In connection with the Southern Alberta tract, no proper government inspection and report was made, the reports of engineers of that company were used when the stock was marketed and when the shareholders' engineers took charge and began to examine the scheme, it was found to be utterly impracticable as an irrigation scheme. This has all been discussed elsewhere, in connection with my report in that matter.
I conclude by saying that this seems to have been really a granting of this particular tract to individual promoters, who looked for enrichment. That they did not make very large sums out of it is not fault of theirs. If these applicants had been informed that the Government policy was such that they must bind themselves to irrigate, that they would not be allowed to sell or dispose of their interests, but that they must irrigate and begin the work and carry it on themselves, it is altogether likely that they never would have endeavoured to acquire this tract. In such an event, in this case, at any rate, these purchasers would not have acquired it, as they would necessarily have taken the trouble to learn, and have learned, that the tract could not be irrigated,
It is satisfactory to learn from this report that the country did not suffer very much if it suffered at all, in connection with this matter. I deny absolutely the charge that I was an intermediary, that the negotiations passed through my hands. Although my memory is a blank as to the circumstances, I say without hesitation that that charge is false. I appeal to the sense of fair play of every man in this House as to whether it was not the duty of the

commissioner, if any insinuations were to be made against me, to allow me to make an explanation in the matter. I would have produced my correspondence and allowed him to overhaul everything in order to find out the truth. Constitutionally, whether or not the transaction is wrong, I have to take the responsibility, and I do not intend to disclaim that responsibility.
I am not here to ask favours from anybody;
I am here simply to uphold my rights as a citizen of Canada, and to defend the good name which I have preserved through a pretty long life. As to what was done under the administration of the late Government, it is open to hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House to make what charges they can make, to find out what has been wrong, if anything, and to have restitution made to the Treasury if the Treasury has suffered by anything that we did. As I say, I am not here to ask any favours, but certainly, as a citizen of Canada and as a member of this House, I am entitled to justice and fair play at the hands of hon. gentlemen opposite.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
I have not had an opportunity of reading the whole of this bulky report in connection with the Aylwin irrigation tract, which has been debated this afternoon and this evening in the House, but my attention has been called to a synopsis of the report which was published by the Ottawa Journal. I have read that synopsis, and it is because my name happens to be mentioned therein that I wish to offer a few remarks in connection with this matter. I suppose this synopsis was carefully prepared, and represents substantially the evidence adduced at the investigation held by Mr. Ferguson.
Let me first read the evidence on which Mr. Ferguson bases the conclusion wherein he connects the name of the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and my own name with this matter. I call the attention of my fellow members
9 p.m. to the evidence given by Mr. Robert in the presence of the commissioner, as follows:
Commissioner: Did you interview the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) up to that time?
Mr. Robert: Oh, I may have. It is quite probable I did.
Commissioner: What other members?
Mr. Robert: At this moment I can't recollect, but I think I may have seen Mr. Lemieux, the member for the district.
Commissioner:	That is the Hon. Rodolphe
Lemieux?
Mr. Robert: Yes, it is quite probable I would go first to the minister of my district. I do not
know in that interview that is referred to what minister I saw.
I quote the following from the same publication, dealing with the report made by Mr. Ferguson:
Twelve days after the date of that letter the minister took up for the second time the dues-, tion of the consideration of Aylwin's application. Mr. Robert's dealings were not with the man who administered the department, but with two oilier ministers-Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux. His certainty that he could procure the grant is evinced by the fact that within a few weeks after March 18th, 1908, and with knowledge of the action of the Minister of the Interior, he purchased the interests of Mr. C. H. Newton.'
Of course, I could leave the ease as it is summarized here and take my seat, because I see nothing in the evidence to connect my name with this matter. First of all, Mr. Robert does not swear that he had seen me. He says it is probable he may have seen me, but he does not recollect. He says he may have seen the minister of the district. As a matter of fact, you will remember that in 1909 I was not what in political parlance we call the minister of this district or of another district; I was not, at all events, the minister representing the district in which Mr. Robert lived, the district of Montreal. If I was the minister of any district,
I was the minister belonging to the Quebec district. I may say further that I do not know Mr. Aylwin and I did not know of the case until I read of it this evening in the Evening Journal. It is not possible for a member of a Government to remember all the Orders in Council that are passed, knowing that thousands are passed, I will not say monthly, but annually, by the Council. I did not know of that Order in Council. Mr. Robert never spoke to me, because I had no business with him, not being the minister of his district; and I never spoke, I say it with emphasis, to my colleague, the Hon. Mr. Oliver, then Minister of the Interior, as regards this transaction, and I cannot see how Mr. Ferguson can base such a conclusion on the evidence of Mr. Robert. Let me repeat again, to show how unfair are the conclusions of the commissioner.
Q. Mi*. Robert, what other members did you see?-A. At this moment I cannot recollect, but I think I may have seen the Hon. Mr. Lemieux, the minister for the district.
I was not minister for the district.
Q. That is, the Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux?- A. Yes. It is quite probable that I would go first to the minister of my district. I do not know in that interview that is referred to what minister I saw.

How in the name of common-sense, and in the name of fair-play could Mr. FeTguson conclude from that evidence that it was through dealings of the right hon. gentleman and myself that this case was promoted in the Department of the Interior? I say it again, I have had nothing whatever to do with it, and this is the first time I have known of this case-only this evening, by reading what has been published in the 'Ottaw.a press.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
Mr. ^Speaker, in connection with this matter it is not my intention to take up the time of the House for more than a very few minutes. You have seen the bulky reports that have been brought down within the last couple of days, and I think every hon. member on the other side of the House who is-actuated by the ordinary spirit of fair-play will recognize that it is rather a difficult matter for any one to go through these reports and understand them on so short a notice. I am not going here to make any particular complaint of the report that Mr. Ferguson has brought down in so far as my name has been connected with a couple of these transactions, for the simple reason that I do not understand them fully, I have not had time or opportunity to go through them. And I want to say further that these matters have all engaged the attention of this House many years ago. I refer to those with which my name has been connected while I was Commissioner of Dominion Lands. As I have not been Commissioner of Dominion Lands for at least eleven years, it is.all ancient history. It was brought up and dealt with in the House and before the Public Accounts Committee many years ago, and there is nothing new, so far as I know, in these reports. Therefore, I do not intend to take up the time of the House in going into them. If my hon. friends opposite think that by handling these reports and bringing up these old matters again they can do me any particular injury in my constituency, or do the Liberal party any particular injury, why, they are welcome to do so. So far as I am personally concerned, in my own constituency, they are doubly welcome to attempt it. They tried it once, many years ago, and did not make very much of it, simply because there was nothing much to be made of it.
So far as the Craven lands are concerned, and so far as the Brown lease was concerned, the lease was not issued until a year or a year and a half after I left the depart-

ment. I shall not shelter myself behind that in any shape or form. The application was made while I was there, and it was all done according to the usual routine of the regulations. The only criticism, as I understand, that has been made is that the rental was not charged from the time the application was made. I venture to observe, and" the Minister of the Interior will, I think, bear me out, that in no case is rental charged until a lease is granted. In this case the rental was charged when the lease was granted, but not for the time that elapsed between the application for the lease and the time that it was granted.
Some remarks have been made about the selling of the Craven lands at a dollar an acre. Let me point out that the application was made in the year 1899. If my memory serves me aright, the sale was made in 1900 or 1901. At that time it was the practice of the department, where lands in that district were sold, to sell them at a dollar an acre. A dollar an acre was the full value of the land. If my memory is correct-and I am not certain, because this happened some 12 or 15 years ago-some of these lands had been homesteaded twice and abandoned by the homesteaders because they could not fulfil the homestead duties, and because the lands were not worth taking out a patent for, in the judgment of the homesteaders. The lands were subject to overflow from Long lake. Some years the water would recede and there would be a crop of hay on the lands, but in many years there was not a ton of hay. At that time Mr. Brown, who subsequently bought the land, was a farmer in that vicinity. He was also a rancher. He went in for mixed farming. He had a large bunch of cattle and made application to purchase some of these lands and, under the ordinary routine of the department,. he was allowed to purchase some 500 acres at one dollar an acre and he put script on some further area of land, totalling about 1,000 acres. Let me point out that at that very time the Regina and Long Lake Railway Company had a grant of one million or one million and a half acres of especially selected land, dry land, not land subject to overflow; and they were offering those lands at $1.25 an acre and could not sell them. Let me further point out that all through that part of the country where to-day the land is of the greatest value, down along the Sault line in the vicinity of Weyburn, later than the time these lands were purchased by Brown, the Canadian Pacific Railway sold hundreds

of thousands of acres for $2.50 an acre. Three or four years ago ordinary farm lands that had been bought for $2.50 an acre in that part of the country around Weyburn, Yellowgrass and up as far as Rouleau, were transferred at $60 and $70 an acre. Anybody could have gone and picked up the choicest quarter-sections in that part of the country at $3 an acre.
My hon. friend made the statement that this land that Mr. Brown had bought for $1 an acre was sold two or three years afterwards for $25 an acre. My hon. friend is mistaken as to the time that elapsed between the purchase and sale of these lands. They were purchased somewhere about 1901 and 1902 and sold nine or ten years later. There is nothing wonderful about that advance in value.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: The sale, or the expropriation, is shown by the evidence to have taken place in 1906.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: The sale by whom?

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: By Mr. Brown.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
I have not the papers
before me and the Solicitor General may have examined them, but I think he is mistaken when he says the lands were sold by Mr. Brown, or were expropriated in 1906.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: The trial in the Exchequer Court took place in 1909.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
If the Solicitor General
is right that the sale took place in 1906, then I am wrong as to the time that elapsed between the purchase of the lands and the time at which they were expropriated. But you must remember that the price of this land was fixed by the Exchequer Court. I was Commissioner of Dominion Lands at that time, and when the application came before me, as hundreds of others came before me, my decision was to allow Mr. Brown to purchase this land in 1901, or 1902, at the usual price at which lands were sold at that time, namely $1 an acre. I made those decisions in the absolute belief that I was doing exactly right and, after a lapse of ten or twelve years from the time that these transactions took place, I have nothing to take back and I am absolutely satisfied that I then was right. I have no reason whatever to think that I did wrong in my position at that time. It is a very simple matter for a commissioner to come ten or twelve years afterwards and make any sort of a report that he chooses. I am not complaining about the
report. If he wants to make a report of that sort, well and good. We have the report and he has the money for making it. If the Government think it is worth while, well and good. As far as I am concerned, I have nothng to apologize for and nothing to take back in any shape, manner or form. I think I was in a better position to judge at that time than this commissioner is to judge at this time of what was a proper decision to come to on a matter of this kind ten or twelve years ago.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the report of Mr. Ferguson which has bean placed on the Table of the House is a vastly important one. It comprises some eleven different subjects that have been under investigation by him for something over a year. It was laid on the table of the House as soon as we were able to lay it on and I can assure the ex-Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) and all concerned, that there was not, and is not now, any intention to take any advantage whatever by reason of the time at which it was there laid. If it is their desire to have an opportunity later on for a fuller perusal than has been open to them, or for more ample discussion, I am sure that on this side of the House there will be no opposition whatever. Any suggestion that may come from them in that regard will be met in the frendliest spirit by us.
I have never been able to appreciate the force of the contention that because a subject is up before us for discussion at the latter end of a session necessarily it must be slurred over and improperly considered. The latter end of the session should be of as much importance to us, and its hours should be made as valuable to us and to the country, as are those of any other part. It is complained this afternoon that we have pretty much finished the other business, that the Estimates are voted, that even that long protracted consideration of the Act for soldiers' votes is over and that, inasmuch as we have no other business to transact, we cannot afford now to give time to the subject under discussion. I would have thought the argument would have proven the other way, that as we are now freed for the most part from the ordinary matters of public concern, we can devote our minds simply and solely to this subject and that there is no reason in the world to hurry until we are through with it, until all have had their say and have had time to say it.

1 rise to address the House on the subject of this report, the debaite having been introduced by the motion of the one hon. member of this House most concerned, the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). I arise in no spirit of personal antipathy to him, nor indeed to any hon. member concerned. Since I have had a seat in Parliament there is no associate in ithis House on either side with whom my personal relations have been more cordial than they have been with the hon. member for Edmonton. At the same time the subjects in the discussion of which his name appears are subjects of public concern and we would never do our duty if by reason of any personal relations we omitted to state the plain facts that appear in those subjects and make known to thp country our opinions and the course of conduct we intend to take regarding them.
It is complained on the other h^nd by the hon. member for Assinaboia (Mr. Turriff) that he has not had time to review the report. The report, or a large part of it, has been on the table since Saturday morning last; the rest of it has been on the fable since Monday morning last and it is now Wednesday night. His complaint also is that the subjects are too old and that in so far as his connection with them is concerned the discussion has very little interest for him at all because he is utterly unable to remember anything about these matters and that the records consequently are all we can rely on and if the records are against him he is satisfied and it has to go aJt that. We are not going to meet that objection of the hon. member for Assiniboia certainly by any further delay. The longer we continue the discussion the stronger the objection will become.
What are the subjects before us and why axe they here ? It was thought at one time that the session of Parliament upon which we are launched, and which is now nearing its conclusion, would be a non-controversial session.
If that had been carried out, if the Opposition had made it possible for the Government to have carried out that intention, then indeed, in my opinion, this report could not have been presented. But, has the course of conduct (of the Opposition been such that it was open for us to choose? From the opening of this session cto the close, their course of conduct has been such that never since the Government was returned to power has

the spirit of partisanship been so aroused and excited as it has been by them. There is no trick of party controversy to which they have not resorted, and by means of their press chiefly, as well as by their speeches in Parliament, they have been endeavouring by uistortion and by every other unworthy resort to cast aspersions on hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, and to make for themselves weapons for an election. And if there is one hon. gentleman more than another who has addressed himself with assiduity to that task, and has never waited for the verdict of committees, and has never waited for the evidence, to come to a conclusion, but who has been Teady in advance to find everybody on this side guilty of everything charged by hon. gentlemen opposite, and to denounce us with adjectives and language that he only can command, it is the hon. member for Edmonton. The language which he adopts to-night, in reference to the commissioner who has made this report-a report so fully substantiated by the evidence produced that even the hon. member for Assiniboia says the has no fault to find with it-the language he has adopted to-night in castigation of that commissioner has been equalled only by the language he has hurled across the floor at ourselves, ever since the opening of this session. He tells us to-night that the revelations here laid before the people of Canada by Mr. Ferguson are so trivial and reflect so little on him and on the Government of which he was a member, and reflect so little on the department over which he presided, that it amounts in fact to a certificate of character upon which he is ready to appeal to the people of Canada.
I want to examine this certificate of character, and I take it that if this is the certificate upon which hon. gentlemen opposite purpose to appeal, then what is revealed here is the character of administration which the people of Canada may expect if they send hon. gentlemen opposite back to office.
The disclosures that are first revealed in the report have to do with lands in western Canada; they have chiefly to do with lands in the very district from which I come. I have not been unfamiliar for many years gone by with the character of transactions revealed in this first report. I heard about them in the last election contest:
I heard more about them, in the contest that preceded the last. Throughout those campaigns, it was reported to me over and over again that we might just as well cease our

efforts to succeed in the Riding Mountain district and in the Dauphin country, because the homestead frauds perpetrated there were such that the Liberal party had a grip on the vote.
The light hon. the ex-Prime Minister tells us that the doings of his Government iand of its departments are open to investigation, and that if we find anything wrong we have a right to reveal it and to demand restitution. Yes, the doings of his Government are open to investigation now; they became open to investigation on the 10th of October, 1911, when he threw down the seals of office and when the right hon. gentleman who now honours the post of Prime Minister took them up. But prior to that day, they were not open to investigation; prior to that day he and his followers behind him, over and over again, resisted motions, resisted resolutions, resisted every effort made by us as we sat in Opposition to have the very subjects which are here revealed investigated by committees of this House. Resolution after resolution, and motion after motion, calling for commissions to investigate these very subjects, were voted down at the right hon. gentleman's behest, and now because we have investigated them at the very first opportunity we had, the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) comes forward and says: there is nothing at all to investigate as regards several of them at least, because the men who committed the frauds are out of office.
What were these frauds in the Riding Mountain district? The hon. gentleman tells us that they are nothing in which the country is concerned at all. Why? Because he says that all these lands were open to homesteading anyway, and that if these fellows did not get them somebody else would, and the country would not have them, and, therefore, we have no concern. That is the attitude assumed to-day by the hon. member for Edmonton. There was a Riding Mountain forest reserve, that skirted the northern portion of my constituency, and the southern portion of the constituency of the member for Dauphin (Mr. Cruise). That forest reserve was defined by legislation of years gone by. It was found, according to the definition of that legislation, that there were large acreages that were not adapted to forestry at all, and that consequently should be thrown open for homesteads. The farmers of the district and all other districts observed-and doubtless some of them were advised in advance by hon. gentlemen opposite and by the minister of the day,-that it was altogether likely that certain portions would subsequently become open for homestead entry. Many became squatters upon lands in that district; some became squatters upon lands within the territory that afterwards became the restricted area of the forest reserve, and others again became squatters on lands which afterwards were thrown outside the new limitation of the forest reserve. With these men it became the duty of the ministry of the day to deal, and when it was determined to throw open for entry the lands outside the new restricted area of the reserve the squatters on those lands became entitled to priority of entry by virtue of the regulations then in force. There were squatters inside the new limits, there were squatters outside the new limits, and what was the policy pursued by the hon. member for Edmonton, then Minister of the Interior? He selects one of hi3 henchmen, a man who was appointed to office for his services to the Liberal party, and one of the most pronounced partisans that ever infested western Canada, a man who to-day stands as admitting under oath that he used his office altogether to advance the interests of the Liberal party and for no other purpose at all; the then Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) invests this man with uncontrolled authority by letter, and he notifies the agent of Dominion Lands to the effect that W. A. Davis, a forest ranger, appointed by his Government, could go on his own will hither and thither, and any man that he recommended for an entry in that new forest reserve or without that new reserve should get that entry without any further inquiry whatsoever. Yet the hon. member tells us that that is .something with which the country is not concerned at all, because, as he says, if he did not give the lands to Shis friends somebody else would get them. What did Davis do? He goes to the printing press and he gets printed several hundred orders addressed to F. K. Herchmer, Esq., saying: "Please permit
Mr. 
to enter for 

lands, and this is
your authority; signed W. A. Davis, forest ranger."
He hands these to Mr. Samuel Cohen and to Mr. Albert McLeod, selected, as he admits, because they are the very best party workers he knows, and these men take these blanks, and they utilize them as an engine of the Liberal party to award the public lands of this country to henchmen of the party in Manitoba. If there is a weapon within the grip of a Government

which illegitimately and illegally used will be certain to corrupt the electorate for election purposes, it is the weapon of these Dominion lands. Was there any restraint put upon Mr. Davis? There was not the least; he had the minister's own authority for what he did; the minister was at the Dominion Lands office at the time he did it, and the minister, sitting in the Dominion Lands .office, wrote him a letter which ratified his authority to do it. He goes on with the work, and hundreds of men who had no right to entries whatever, are given entry for Dominion lands by the authority of the then Minister of the Interior of Canada. Amongst these men is one gentleman, now an hon. member of this House, a man who has done nothing wrong at all, says the ex-Minister of the Interior, but a man whom his own henchman, Mr. Davis, swore got an entry under that system to which he had no right whatever under the law. What does Mr. Cruise do? He goes up to the Riding Mountain reserve and picks up a good quarter-section, although the reserve is not thrown open for entry yet. Does he build a house on it and reside on it and become a squatter prior to the throwing open for entry? Not at all. He builds four walls without a roof; he does not live on the quarter-section for a day; and, after he gets the four walls up, he thinks that he has done enough, and he comes back to his farm in Dauphin; and up to the time he made his entry, yes, up to the time he got his patent, he had not lived on the quarter-section, and how could he be a squatter if he did pot live on it? He gets the entry, but he is no worse than hundreds of others who get entries in the same manner; and the man responsible and the man guilty, is not half so much Mr. Cruise or the other men who availed themselves of the rewards of this system as the then Minister of the Interior, who permitted, authorized and ratified the system after he knew what was going on, and who accepted the results of the system in the election of 1908. Let me put this to the right hon. the leader of the Opposition: What does he think of the management of the Department of the Interior under his regime by the hon. gentleman Opposition: what does he think of the management is now shown to have been used by the then minister and by his henchmen for the purpose of electing the Liberal representative of Dauphin aud for no other purpose whatever? Does the leader of the Opposition think he is entitled to the votes
fMr Meighen.l
of the Liberal member for Dauphin which have been given obediently at his command for the Liberal party in this House all through this Parliament, after he sees how those votes were got under the system which has been revealed ? I suffered from this system also; men from my own county were promised by this man and by his henchmen homesteads in the Dauphin district if they would support the Liberal nominee. These promises were made over and over again, and I lost votes by them, and those votes were bribed and paid for under the authority of the hon. member for Edmonton. The letters are on record, and there are others here in the evidence which are not on record, but which are not essential to the proof. It is not a matter of dispute; the man who did this work swore that he did it and told why he did it. He allowed himself to be made a tool of his party; and when he was under oath, he was ready to admit it. He employed two men, Cohen and McLeod, because he said that they could not be beaten in the country for seeing to it that wherever the party would get an advantage, they would give it the advantage, and when he was asked: "were you not just the same?" the answer was:	" Sure." He resigned
shortly after the present Government was installed in office, by the votes of the people of Canada, and I presume his resignation comes within the class of those complained of by hon. gentlemen opposite- those that were made under pressure and that amounted to dismissal, because, as hon. gentlemen opposite say, the men did not get a fair show at all. Yes, Mr. Davis ' resigned, and many others resigned under similar circumstances; but they were retained in office by the ex-Minister of the Interior after he knew, and after the records showed that he knew, the wrong which they perpetrated against the people in Canada and against the voters of that district, by his authority and undeT his supervision. Why did the hon. 'member for Edmonton retain Mr. W. A. Davis as forest ranger after he knew that Mr. Davis had disposed of lands of the people of Canada by the hundreds of acres, by the hundreds of quarter-sections, illegally, fraudulently and for political purposes ? The hon. member for Edmonton is in the same position to-day as if he himself had acted the part of Mr. W. A. Davis, and had awarded homestead entries by the hundred in the Riding Mountain district in order to gain an illegitimate and illegal party advantage over his political

opponents in those parts. If he had dismissed Mr. Davis, if he had called him to account, if he had visited upon him any punishment whatever after he knew the facts, then he might have absolved himself. Did he know the facts? He did not deny this afternoon that he knew the facts; he knew of the deeds when they were being perpetrated; they were brought to his attention at the time, and the letters are on the file. He kept Mr. Davis in office, however, and he thereby added his seal to the wrongs perpetrated by Mr. Davis in that district.
But the Davis case is not all; the Cruise case is not all; there are ten more and they seem to grow in importance, each one over the one before it. We come next to the Pedley ease. Mr. Pedley is dismissed,. it is true, or he has resigned-I do not know which, and I do not think it makes much difference. Mr. Pedley has resigned and because he has resigned, the hon. member for Edmonton says: you do not need any report on this matter at all; why do you send Mr. Ferguson after Mr. Pedley when Mr. Pedley is not an officer of the department? Nobody knows better than the hon. member for Edmonton that, when Mr. Ferguson started -out after Mr. Pedley, and when he acquired a knowledge of these nefarious transactions, Mr. Pedley was still Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, and the reason why he does not hold that position any longer is this, that as soon as the facts were revealed by the Ferguson report, he threw down the seals and fled from his office as from a hissing -snake; but he would not be out of his position to-day if it had not been for Mr. Ferguson and Mr. Ferguson's report, and according to the hon. member for Edmonton he should not be out of his position yet. Does he condemn the transactions of Mr. Pedley? Did he do so when he was on his feet this afternoon? No, Mr. Pedley had not one word of criticism at my hon. friend's hands. Speak about certificates of character! My hon. friend gave Mr. Pedley a certificate of character just as valuable as the one Mr. Ferguson gave him. Why, he said, Mr. Pedley is an honourable man; he can stand up and look the Prime Minister of Canada or anybody else in the face. Be is a friend of Mr. Pedley's still. And, Sir, Mr. P-edley, the man found guilty on hi-s own evidence, is to-day in the employ of the Liberal party, their organizer in Northern Ontario. Mr. Pedley is out of office to-day; there is no doubt about that.
He got out of office very quickly, as soon as he was found out, and he will be out of office until a certain day and no longer- the day when the Liberal party is restored to power in this Dominion. Then he will get his reward the same as Wagner got his reward, the same as many others got their rewards, when the ex-Minister of the Interior was in office.
Mr. Pedley in the year 1902 received applications for grazing leases in the Blood reserve. He got one in December of that year from Mr. McLaughlin -and Mr. Millar, of Toronto. These men were in correspondence with Mr. Pedley for this grazing lease. As a result of that correspondence and of an interview with Mr. Pedley of the 21st of April following, they came to the conclusion that they were entitled to the lease and proceeded to arrange their affairs accordingly. They proceeded to secure a number of cattle to stock the land, and to employ a foreman and to prepare to take possession, believing that the lease was at hand and that they were the first and were entitled to it. What happened? The interview to which I have referred was on the 21st April. On the 22nd April an application comes in by Mr. Donald Mc-Ewan of the city of Brandon, asking for a grazing lease for the same land. On the 6th of the same month Mr. Pedley, at the request of a legal firm in Ottawa, acting supposedly for this same Donald McEwan, wrote Mr. McEwan a letter authorizing him to go upon the reserve and make any arrangement he could with the Indians inhabiting the reserve. It was apparently his intention, as far back as the 6th of that month, to grant this grazing lease to McEwan. On the 22nd, after he had written the letter, the application comes in. Now, this application of Donald McEwan is revealed by the evidence to be really the application of Peter Ryan, of Toronto, who used the name of McEwan and gave McEwan four shares of the stock of -the company for the use of hi-s name. Mr. Peter Ryan, of the city of Toronto, is shown to be a close friend of the-Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs. So close friends are they that when Mr. Ryan is hard up he draw's and kites upon Mr. Pedley, and when Mr. Pedley is hard up he operates through Mr. Ryan. Such is the evidence given by Mr. Ryan himself. That has been going on for some years. So Mr. Ryan comes along with the-application in the name of Donald McEwan; and from that hour until now

Messrs. McLaughlin & Millar, those who have rights by priority, are hurled to the winds, and Mr. Ryan is the only man considered. Why? There is a declaration of trust set out in the evidence verbatim, produced and made an exhibit, which shows that Mr. Peter Ryan held this 6 per cent of the stock of the company that was to get the lease for Mr. A. C. Bedford-Jones, a lawyer of the city of Toronto. And there is a declaration by Mr. Bedford-Jones, who takes the 6 per cent, naming himself as trustee, and stating that he holds that f>
per cent for Frank Pedley, of the city of Ottawa-a declaration of trust not made in writing, and exposable in writing, but made by Mr. Bedford-Jones, according to his evidence under oath, and latterly admitted by Mr. Frank Pedley himself.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: Who is Mr. Pedley?

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
Mr. Pedley at that time was the Deputy Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs under the Government of that day; he was the man who had the granting of these leases; he is the man who turned McLaughlin and Millar down, and took Mr. Peter Ryan, under the name of Donald McEwan, as the proper party to get the lease. Six per cent of the stock Mr. Bedford-Jones holds as trustee. These facts are brought before Mr. Frank Pedley in evidence. He is confronted with the declaration by the commissioner that he was the real owner of that 6 per cent. What does he do? He denies it under oath- never heard of it; did not know anything about it; denies it over page after page of the evidence. I can read his denial. 1 turn to page 15 of his evidence:
Q. Were you ever offered by Peter Ryan or any person on his behalf, or on behalf of Donald McEwan or Donald McEwan and Company, any interest in that privilege of concession?-A. No, never.
Q. And you never acquired any interest in it?-A. No, I did not.
Q. Do you know of any officer or official either in the Indian Department-I am putting it correctly, when I say Indian Department, am I not?-A. Yes.
Q. Well, do you know of any officer or official in the Indian Department who acquired any interest in it directly or indirectly either from Donald McEwan, Peter Ryan, or any person else?-A. I do not.
Q. Now, referring to these documents. I see in one of the documents to which i have just referred, dated 10th October, 1904, of which Peter Ryan of Toronto is the party of the first part and Alban C, Bedford-Jones party of the second part, Jones is set out there to be
trustee. You see that, do you not?

A. Yes,
I see that.
Q. I wish to know from you if you know for whom Jones was trustee?-A. I do not.
fMr. Meighen.j
Q. Jones is on the face of that document apparently trustee for some person?-A. Yes.
Q. Now I ask you if you can help me to ascertain who that person is for whom he was trustee.-A. No, I do not know anything about it. The first time these documents came to us would be as per the date of Millar's letter, the 17th December, 1912.
Q. I see by these documents to which I am referring and in which Alban C. Bedford-Jones is trustee that he acquired from Peter Ryan as trustee six per cent of the total profits resulting from the enterprise which Ryan assigns him?-A. Yes.
Q. The enterprise referred to, as appears by this document, is the ranching enterprise on the Blood Indian Reserve granted to Donald McEwan?-A. Yes.
And later on:
Q. I put it to you that when Jones received that cheque of $1,000 from Charles Millar, he gave you, if not the entire sum, a portion of it, did he?-A. No. .
Q. You say you had no interest in it at all? [DOT]-A. I beg your pardon?
Q. You say you had no interest in it at all? 

A. No, no interest at all.
Q. And you never received any part of that thousand dollars?-A. No.
Pretty strong evidence, pretty strong swearing by this gentleman who could look anybody in the face, even the Prime Minister of Canada. I quote further from his evidence:
Q. Then Peter Ryan was not indebted to you in any money at the time of the assignment of this 6 per cent interest to A. C. Bedford Jones?-A. Oh, no.
Q. So that that could not have been given by Ryan to A. C. Bedford-Jones in payment of any moneys which he owed to you?-A. No, it could not.
Q. Is it possible that Peter Ryan assigned this interest to you in the Blood .Indian reserve to pay any moneys he owed you?-A. No.
Q. I am referring to the agreement between Peter Ryan and A. C. Bedford-Jones of the 10th October, 1904, and I show you the papers. That is the paper to which we have been referring in your examination this morning, which purports to be a copy of the agreement of the 10th of October, 1904, between Peter Ryan of the first part and A. C. Bedford-Jones, trustee, of the second part. This is the agreement to which we were referring this morning?-A. Yes.
Q. I am now saying that that was not given by Peter Ryan and could not have been given by Peter Ryan for any moneys he owed you? -A. No.
Q. Or for any indebtedness of Peter Ryan to you?-A. No.
It is apparent that no matter how often the question was repeated; he was ready with a denial of the suggestion that he ever had the slightest interest in that lease; that he ever had the slightest interest in Mr. Bedford-Jones's trusteeship; that he ever received a dollar from him; that on account of any business relations between

him and Peter Ryan there could have been an .assignment of that interest for him, or a declaration of that interest as held in trust for him. I quote further:
Q. Was there any dealing between you and Peter Ryan or anybody on his behalf whereby you should receive or that anybody should receive on your behalf that 6 per cent interest? -A. No, there was not.
This is important evidence, in the light of the facts which are revealed a few pages further on.
Q. Had you any understanding about any per cent of interest?-A. No.
Q. With any person?-A. No.
Q. What does Jones mean when he says he remitted you out of the moneys which Charles Millar paid him, a certain portion of that money?-A. Well, it means I did not get it, if he remitted it.
Lost in the mails.
Q. Had you any knowledge that he was making a remittance to you of any money, or that he ever did make a remittance of any such moneys?-A. No.
What turns up a little later? Mr. Bedford-Jones is again examined; Mr. Bedford-Jones produces his cheques, and then the commissioner comes back to Mr. Pedley, who, as the hon. member says, using the words of Mark Antony, is an " honourable man." Page 28:
Q Now, you got $1,000 in money; that is to say you got $900 in 1908?-A. Yes.
Q. And Mr. Jones kept $100 for his services, which he charged against you out of the $1,000? -A. Yes.
Q. So that you practically got $1,000 of the money?-A. Yes.
Later he endeavours to make an explanation. Oh, he says, I was endorsing certain notes for Mr. Ryan, and I took this $1,000 as security that he would pay the notes. It is a form of business transaction entirely new to me-perhaps the hon. member for Edmonton has heard of it before-where a man who endorses a note for another takes the other man's cash by way of security. There is page after page of explanation here by this " honourable man " to the effect that Mr. Peter Ryan, instead of paying his debts, chose to draw upon Mr. Frank Pedley for a few hundred dollars and then pay Mr. Frank Pedley money with which he might have paid his debts. High finance! frenzied finance! but a form of finance thought of by Mr. Frank Pedley when he was giving his evidence, and not before. I quote further from his evidence:
Q. Does Peter Ryan owe you any money today?-A. Well, In that sense he does. I am on his paper to-day.
Q. To whait extent?-A. I think it is three or four hundred dollars.
Q. If Mr. Ryan took up that four hundred dollars to-day or to-morrow, then you would not have to pay any of it?-A. If he took that up, of course, my account would be relieved to that extent.
Q. Then would Mr. Ryan be entitled to receive back the sum of $1,000?-A. As far as I am concerned, be would.
Here is Mr. Frank Pedley, an honourable man, holding the $1,000 which he says is Peter Ryan's, and holding it for fear Peter Ryan will not pay a $400 note upon which Frank Pedley is endorser. Did it ever occur to Mr. Frank Pedley that possibly $400 of Peter Ryan's money might have been remitted to Peter Ryan and that Peter Ryan could then have taken up his note and have become entitled to the other $600? I wonder why that never occurred to these great business intel-10 p.m. lects, Mr. Peter Ryan and Mr. Frank Pedley. I will tell you why it never occurred to them: because the $1,000 was Mr. Frank Pedley's money; he got it for giving the preference to his friend, Peter Ryan. Does the hon. member for Edmonton believe anything else? He knew of this transaction. He has read the evidence; he gave some of it this afternoon.

What does the hon.

speechtext: That is when he was down here attending committees of Parliament in order to get campaign literature.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: I think the hon. member is quite right.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
These are the doings of Mr. Frank Pedley. Because he was found out and because he chased himself out of the office as soon as he was found out, the hon. member tells the House that we should not have started the commissioner on his trail; that it was not worth the money to ascertain that a man holding a responsible position as head of the Indian Department of this country, under the Minister of the Interior, was a man of the calibre and character of Mr. Frank Pedley ; to ascertain that wie country was well rid of his services. Is $30,000 too much for that truth alone?
But Mr. Frank Pedley's depredations did not end there. He thought of another scheme. At the time he thought of this he was not Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, but he did hold an important office in the Department of the Interior. The other man associated with him was the Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, and had to do directly with the lands concerned in this transaction.
Did anybody ever conceive of such a scheme as this ? Here is Mr. J. A. Smart, Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs in the Government of Canada, afterwards promoted for his efficiency, no doubt, to the office of Deputy Minister of Militia.
Here is J. A. Smart, charged with the disposition of the Indian lands of this country under the law and under the minister. He forms a partnership with Mr. Pedley, in the department, and with Mr. White, who has to do with some other branch of the service
immigration, ,1 believe. They are the men who open the tenders in connection with the sale of Indian lands. They are the men and the only men-the public have no access or insight-they were the men who have access and insight into all data as to the value of those lands and who know the tenders that are received. They form a company, they employ the same Mr. Bedford-Jones, trustee, of the city of Toronto. First of all they do not become incorporated, they are just a body of associates, a sort of family compact. They go down to Mr. Bedford-Jones and arrange with him that, at a figure that they shall name and on receipt of their instructions, he shall put in tenders for 45,000 acres of Indian lands in the Moose mountains. And on a certain date, just as the time is up to close all tenders for In-

dian lands, Mr. Bedford-Jones sends a telegram to Mr. Smart: "Package received,- everything arranged for all right." I think I have that pretty close. The exact words are:
Package received, suitable party procured, instructions understood. Complete matter tomorrow.
A. C. Bedford-Jones.
Language intended to be mysterious, but indeed very clear to any one who has read telegrams of this kind. Afterwards Mr. Jones admits that the package received was a lot of tenders filled in by these same gentlemen in the office of the Minister of the Interior, the price at which they were to buy filled in. And then they, having hied themselves back to the city of Ottawa, open-their own tenders and award the lands to themselves ! Oh, says the hon. member for Edmonton, they had to be the highest bidder or they could not get it, and if they did not get it they_ went down the same as anybody else. They went down? They put in,
I think, three or four hundred tenders, and all their tenders were accepted but eight or ten. What excellent guessers they were of the price at which they might get Indian lands !

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: Who accepted them?

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
Who accepted them?
They accepted them themselves, they" were the buyers and the sellers, they were dealing with these lands as trustees, dealing with the property over which they were trustees. These are the honourable men whose conduct in this matter to the hon. member for Edmonton is ratified by him and he declares that, having done it, they can look any man in Canada in the face. This is the man taken up by the Liberal party and sent over Canada to organize for their victory and his own victory and re-instatement in office at and after the next election. They did not confine themselves to the Indian lands of Moose mountain, they went into other lands. But in Moose mountain alone they bought some 45,000 acres of land and they paid for that land in November, 1901, $54,850. As I remember they did not pay up for quite a while after that; I think they paid it out of the sale price, putting up a little in the meantime. They bought it in November, 1901, for $54,850 and sold it in April, 1902, for $112,500. They make a profit on these lands of $57,150 in three or four months, dealing with lands for which they are trustees under the Government of Canada, dealing with them unfairly,

illegally, illegitimately as against other tenderers and as against, the (people of this country. They pocket the money, the result and the reward of their nefarious transaction, and they get the imprimatur of the bon. member for Edmonton for doing so. There may be fraud perpetrated under this Government, there may be parties in one extremity of Canada or the other who abuse the trust imposed in them; but there has been a Government in office since the 10th day of October, 1911, who, when they find out that these frauds are perpetrated and who the perpertrators are, do not stand at the door and block, do not render immune from punishment, do not reward for their offences, but who pursue them and punish them, and where legally possible, recover the money for the people of Canada.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: When lias the Government done it?

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
When has the Government done it? There is one unfortunate thing, I do not know whether the hon. member for Prescott wall! be able to fully get his mind about this, but there is one unfortunate fact that the Government of to-day legally is the successor of the Government of yesterday; that when the Government of yesterday does a certain act and it is ratified by the then minister, the Government of to-day is bound by it. But there are men who do not come within the protection of that rule, -and I do not think the hon. member for Prescott will be quite so anxious to spring the subject of restitution when he comes back to Parliament-if he ever does again.
Another transaction was referred to and admitted by the hon. member for Edmonton this evening. I do -not wish to delay the House by going over -aJll these matters; other members of the House have read them also. They have been exposed to view, open to perusal for days. But there -is one matter to which I wish to r-efeT because -it has been covered in the speech of the hon. member for Edmonton. In the year 1905 the hon, member was and had been many years proprietor of the Edmonton Bulletin, a newspaper published in his own city, a newspaper which, since its inception, had been the personal -asset-, had been the personal organ of the hon. member for Edmonton. That has been known from end to end of Canada -as his own personal organ, as the particular engine of publicity by which he has effected, from time to time, his recurring elections to this House. The Edmonton Bulletin becomes incorporated in 1905.
The bon. member has an interest- in it and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company come along and subscribe $15,000 to the Edmonton Bulletin and become stockholders -to that extent. Now, what are the circumstances? Why did they do so? Is there any ground of -offence, any cause of offence in that transaction? Is it something upon which the people of the country should look with favour or with frown, and why? The Grand Trunk Pacific was incorporated in 1903, incorporated for specific and definite purposes by an Act of this Parliament. I have read its charter a-nd I am not able to find in it that a part of its purpose or a portion of its power consisted in running newspapers. I have not been able to -ascertain even that it had the power, that it had the legal capability, of investing any of its funds 'in newspaper enterprises. But in the year 1903, they -make a contract with the people of Canada, the most important, one of the most momentous and by far the most disastrous into which the people of this country ever entered; a contract by virtue of which they have extracted with regularity millions and millions from the treasury of this country. They make their contract in 1903, they secure a modification of the contract hugely -to their own advantage in 1904. This they secured at the hands of the Government, of which the present leader of the Opposition was the head. They come back in the year 1905, they amend the contract again, they come back in 1906, and still important concessions are made to the Grand Trunk Pacific. Objection was taken to that contract from the first on the part of the Opposition of that day, strong objection was taken to it on the part of the distinguished leader of the Opposition of that day, but at every point at which the Opposition of that time sought to amend the contract in the interests of the people they were met with the assertion on the part of the then leader of the Government that a contract was a contract and that it was too late to change it whether to the advantage of the people of Canada or not. But it was changed. It was cast iron as against the people of Canada but it was soft and plastic as against the Grand Trunk Pacific. They came back in 1904, 1905 and 1906 and they got $5,000,000 of cash that had lain in the Treasury as security transferred and reincarnated into $5,000,000 of bonds, and they got the power to declare their parent, the Grand Trunk Railway Company, to be the owners by virtue of an ad-

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
There is no subject comprised and treated of within the four corners of the Ferguson report that is not of as much importance, and that does not reveal just as astounding details as does this. But more than that; more than has been revealed within the four corners of the report, is the astounding pronouncement read from the files of the Interior Department to Parliament and to the country by the Minister of the Interior in this House to-night. What shall we hear about that? What will be the pronouncement of the leader of the Opposition on that? Can it be said that the hon. member for Edmonton made a mistake? I may say that I thought so myself when I first heard it. I do not think any member of this House was more surprised than I. If there is one man within the four corners of Canada who should have
known	and	did	know the facts,	it was thehead	of	the department	who	hadto do with such transactions. One would expect that a farmer who got a patent	for	a	quarter-section	and	whowould	read	in	his patent that	the	mines
and minerals were reserved, would know that they were reserved, and every farmer does know it. One would have expected that the minister of the department, who himself reserved them, would also know that they were reserved. But one would certainly be doubly sure that he who was both the patentee and the minister would know that the mines and minerals were reserved. And knowing that they were reserved, and knowing that in these minerals he had no interest whatever, and knowing that he had no part or portion of proprietorship in these minerals, it is astonishing to find that the minister, who is the patentee, should affect to deal with these minerals, and did deal with them, and that he in his personal capacity, instead of as a minister of the Crown, receives a royalty month after month and year after year, and never . accounts for that royalty. It is an astonishing pronouncement. I do not think there was any porch-climbing to get it; it was revealed on the face of the.file. I do not know in that case who the thug was, but there it stands. It might never have been known if the hon. member had not come forward, when his Government were hurled from office, and ask for a lease of the mineral rights, but he came forward and asked for a lease in November, 1911, and that lease is there, and since November, 1911, everything is open to the face of day, and that revealed what had gone on before in Oliver's time. The minister never disclosed to the Crown, of which he had the honour to be a minister, and never disclosed to the people, of whose wealth and whose assets he was the trustee, that he was collecting and pocketing money that was not his but theirs, and to which he had no right.
I opened my remarks by saying that there was no necessity, and no attempt on our part to hurry this matter at all. It is a matter of pressing importance, and it is my desire, and I speak the wishes of hon. members on this side I am sure, that every opportunity to defend or explain be given the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley), or any other hon. gentleman opposite -and I mention the hon. member for St. John merely because I see him at times coming close to the hon. member for Edmonton, and I know of no better wrecking-tug in the Opposition than is the

hon. member for St. John. It is our desire that the utmost opportunity of defence be given, and there is no purpose to the contrary. This is before Parliament, and almost this alone is before Parliament, and we on our part are prepared to stay here and discuss it, and if necessary to revive from day to day this discussion, until the fullest justice is done to all concerned.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: I cannot fail to respond to the invitation of the Solicitor General to make a few remarks on this motion which was made by my hon. friend from Edmonton. I was not quite able to hear the description the Solicitor General gave of me, but I thought he said I was a good wrecking something.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: Wrecking-tug.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: He did not say you were a thug.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: I may be able to rescue a good many things, hut I do not know that I could rescue gentlemen on the- other side of the House from the hole into which they have fallen this session. Whatever else I would be willing to do, I would be very sorry to undertake that job. There is something peculiar about these attacks which the Solicitor General and the Minister of the Interior have made to-night. I was particularly struck with the remark of the Minister of the Interior when he said that he was a man of peace, and a man of moderate views, and the gave the House to understand that he would not have made this attack upon the ex-Minister of the Interior if it were not for certain statements which had been made by the Liberal members of this House during the last few weeks. I suppose the Minister of the Interior was referring to the disclosures which have been -made in the committee about boots, and t'hir disclosures in the committee on public accounts about binoculars, and bandages, and drugs, and horses-

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: And jams.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
Yes, and jams. I suppose that what the Minister of the Interior means is that in consequence of the very strong remarks which have been made by members on this side of the House and by newspapers in the country, he felt constrained to make an attack on the ex-Minister of the Interior, which he would not otherwise believe it to be his duty to make. That also explains the very warm attack which has been made upon the hon. member (Mr. Oliver) by the
[Mr Meighen.]
Solicitor General. In other words, they are trying to draw a red herring across the track; they are trying to divert the minds of the people of this country from the disclosures which have been made during the last few weeks by seeking to revive not only ancient history but ancient romance. The Solicitor General and the Minister of the Interior have referred to the report made by Mr. Ferguson, and they stated that it has been brought down just as soon as it was reasonably possible to do so.
Is this quite accurate? We have the fact that for about three years-scarcely long enough to earn $40,000-Mr. Ferguson has been engaged in these investigations, and we have a right to assume that many of these reports were ready a good many months ago and that many of them might have been laid upon the table of the House at the commencement of this session of Parliament; but it looks to me as if they had been reserved for some such occasion as this-as if hon. gentlemen opposite thought that there was scandal in the air in connection with these war expenditures and that disclosures would be made which would shock the people of this country, and as if they kept this report back until the last moment, hoping to bring it down at a time when there would be scanty opportunity of answering the arguments, when many of the members of the House had gone to their homes and when many more would have so completed their arrangements to go home that it would be at very great inconvenience that they could remain here.
Speaking particularly to the charge which has been made with respect to a homestead entry granted to Mr. Cruise, the hon. member for one of the constituencies in Manitoba, there is not any ground whatever for reflection upon the action of the department, because so far as the department and the late Minister of the Interior are concerned, all the requirements of the law were complied with. The allegation is that Mt. Cruise purchased upon credit some seven cattle in order to make the number up to 20, and that, alleging that he was possessed of 20 head of cattle, he was entitled under the law to a homestead entry. It is alleged that in respect of that Mr. Cruise deceived the department; but that shows no fault or irregularity upon the part of the department; it is a charge made against Mr. Cruise. That hon. gentleman, however, went home before this report was brought down, and to him it is very un-

fortunate and unfair that the report should have been held to this late date. Although my hon. friend the Solicitor General says, "we are prepared to stay here and give ample time for this discussion," he knows that upwards of a month ago the Government prepared for an early prorogation, giving notice of .morning sittings, taking .all private days for the discussion of Government measures, and also taking Saturdays.
