"When this is done members begin to make preparations to go home, because they feel that prorogation will take place at an early date, and many members went to uieir homes before this report was brought down.
I am not going at length into these matters; but I want to speak of a charge made that there was an irregularity in connection with a sale of land to Mr. Brown in the valley of the Last Mountain lake. I want to speak of this, because when I have referred to all the facts which have been brought out by Mr. Ferguson, his including this in the list of these scandals which he says he has discovered during his long period of investigation, and it being one of the most important things which he was able (to discover, when hon. gentlemen see the triviality of it and see how groundless is the charge which he makes, they will realize that there is very little in these allegations after all; because ordinarily in the case of an investigation of this character, particularly an ex-parte investigation as these were to a large extent, from one you can very well judge all. When you find that the commissioner has been straining at an effort to discover some one guillty in connection with this matter you can well believe that there is a distorted report in other matters. What are the- facts in reference to this matter? To begin with, the quantity of land bought by Mr. Brown was nbt 1,000 acres, as I understood the Minister of the Interior to say, but only something like 500 acres.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
I stated 530 odd acres at $1 an acre, and the balance making up
1,000	acres on which he placed halfbreed scrip.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend is wrong as to the difference between 530 acres and the 1,000; I think. Mr. Brown was the owner of that land a considerable time before he bought the 530 acres. It will appear in the report of Mr. Ferguson that Mr. Brown was a very large farmer and rancher, owing 170 head of cattle, a large number of horses, -and cultivating a 163
large area of land, being one of the largest farmers in that section of the country. He had bought a very considerable amount of land from The Canada Northwest Land Company that had purchased, a.s my hon. friend knows, from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the original grantee of the Crown; he had bought from people who had obtained patents and altogether he was the owner of about 2,000 acres of land, a part of which was in the valley known as the outlet of the Last Mountain lake. A considerable portion of the land was on a hillside, and a large area of some 400 acres upon the level land at the .top of the valley. He was using all this land together as being a part of his farm. Among the other pieces of land which he had bought, he had acquired out of section 5 in the valley at the foot of the Last Mountain lake 122 acres or thereabouts, which was the only portion of the section which had been surveyed for settlement or sale. When the land was surveyed, it was found that upwards of 500 acres of section 5 was covered by the waters of Last Mountain lake, and so worthless did it ap.peaT to the surveyors that they did not survey it, and they reported it to the department a.s land covered by water. When the Canadian Pacific Railway Company took their grant within the 20-mile belt, they refused to take any part of section 5 except the 122 acres by reason of the fact that the remainder was covered with water. When the survey was made, the valley of Last Mountain lake was usually .pretty well covered with water for a long period in the summer. I know the country very well because I was there in 1883, and at that time the foot of Last Mountain lake was somewhere about four or five miles further to the south and east than it afterwards came. The water of the Last Mountain lake dried up to a certain extent and receded, as was the case with many other lakes in our northwestern country. The result of that was that after a few years, a portion of the remainder of this section 5 became so dry that a quantity of hay could be cut over a considerable part of it in some years; but there was always the danger of recurring floods, and the land was regarded as being of comparatively little value. There was a rule in the West, as it is the rale generally in all of the provinces of Canada, that where a man owns land fronting upon a -lake or river, the Government will not grant what is called the fore-shore of the lake or river to any one but the riparian owner. That land was .left there; and when Mr. Brown as the



riparian owner of these 122 acres applied for the land, it was recognized that he was the proper person to whom the title should be given, if he were willing to pay the ordinary price for land of that quality. After considerable inquiry the value of the land was fixed at $1 an acre, and at that price the land was sold to Mr. Brown. It will be found by the report that negotiations for the purchase were entered upon in 1900. This land formed a part of a very large farm, about two thousand acres, upon which Mr. Brown carried on large farming and ranching operations, on account of which it was desirable for him to get all the hay he could in the valley of the Last Mountain lake. As I have said, the Last Mountain lake had dried up to a considerable extent, and for a good many years all that section of country in the vicinity of the Last Mountain lake, especially the land to the West, was regarded as a dry section in which farming could not be carried on successfully. The railway, the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan, was built from Regina to Prince Albert, going into the valley of the Last Mountain lake, northwards to the west of the lake. And though that road was completed-and I was connected with that road-from 1890 down to 1900, there was no travel to speak of over the road, and it scarcely paid its running expenses. It did not pay interest on its debentures nor anything to shareholders, but barely paid expenses, though it was operated by the Canadian Pacific Railway, and operated as well as any good railway company could operate it. All that district lay stagnant. There were a few enterprising people like Mr. Brown, who engaged in general farming and ranching. They were excellent farmers and ranchmen, and they stayed on in the country in spite of the discouragements which drove many people away. It was not until 1900 that there began to be any development in that section of country. I venture to say that at the time when Mr. Brown bought that land, a considerable portion of which had been previously covered with water-dry in some seasons, but in others covered with water- one dollar an acre was the full value of the land. But what does Mr. Ferguson say with reference to the value? Does he say that this is too little to pay? Not at all; he makes no such charge, although from the argument of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Roche), one would think, if he had not read the report, that the land for which Mr. Brown had paid $1 an acre had been found by the commissioner to be
worth much more. At page 162 of this part of the report, he says:
Whether or not these lands in question were valueless-
Not pretending to know from the evidence whether they were valuable or not.
*-I wish to say that in my opinion the disposal of public lands without full knowledge is an unbusinesslike proceeding which ought not to be permitted.
That is the gravamen of the charge-that, even though this land may not have been worth more than one dollar an acre, even though the price obtained by the department may have been a good one, an improper course was pursued because it was sold without inspection.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
Where does the hon.
gentleman find those words-that the price received by the department was a good one?

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
No; he says:
Whether or not these lands in question were valueless, I wish to say that in my opinion the disposal of public lands without full knowledge of their value is an unbusinesslike proceeding and ought not to be permitted.
I say that is not a finding on the part of Mr. Ferguson that those lands were sold below their value, it is an admission that they may not have been worth more than a dollar an acre. But it says that they ought not to have been sold without a thorough examination so that the department would know their value. Was there not an examination? When the lands were surveyed, the surveyors would go upon every section, and they would make a report stating whether the land was stony or free from stone; the slope of-the land, whether towards the north or in any other direction; the nature of the soil, whether clay, loam or gravelly, and also whether any part of the land was covered by water. And in the files of the department, available every day to the officials, there would be found the report of these surveyors who made a careful examination of this land stating that only 122 acres was such that the Canadian Pacific Railway could fairly be called upon to take it, the rest being covered with water. Surely that was a report upon which the officials of the department could act; and when they were offered $f an acre they were getting, as they thought, a fair and reasonable price	for the land.
As the hon. member for Edmonton has stated, at that time the very best land in the province of Saskatchewan was being sold at from $1 to $2.50 an acre. The rail-

[DOT]2537
way company to which I have referred sold their entire land grant, in respect of the first twenty miles of their railway, for $1 an acre and were glad to get it. Before 1902 the " American invasion " had begun. These experienced farmers had begun to come into that dry section of country. Having had the soil analysed and having knowledge of a process of farming in semidry countries which had then come into vogue, they were satisfied that the land in that country could be cultivated to advantage. As late as 1902, after so many thousands of Americans had come in and shown the capabilities of that country, the very best land, the pick of the land of that whole portion of central Saskatchewan, was under option to my knowledge for a period of three months at $1.50 an acre, and nobody could be got to take up that option or invest in the land. That is the very pick of the whole country which is now the garden of Saskatchewan. The fact that in the years from 1902 to 1910 land kept jumping up in value, rising at the rate of $2 an *acre a year, does not prove that a way back before 1902 that land bought by Mr. Brown had any greater value than $1 an acre.
What happened later which caused the Government to expropriate? Both sides of the Last Mountain lake were rapidly settled by good settlers. One or more steamers having been placed upon the lake, it became necessary-because the water in the lake had fallen to a depth of five or six feet, making it too shallow for the steamers-to undertake a plan to place a dam across the creek which runs out of the lake, and so to hold back the waters and raise the level of the lake for the accommodation of the steamers and to permit the navigation of the lake. Thio is a lake of about 60 miles in length, and its navigation is desirable in the interests of the settlers.. Besides, Last Mountain lake, being a large area of water, was calculated to become a great summer resort for the city of Regina -in fact, it has become such a resort. That is in a country where great lakes and rivers axe comparatively scarce. Undertaking, as we did, the project of increasing and improving the navigation of Last Mountain lake, it became necessary to dam the creek, and in flooding back the waters of the lake we flooded the land owned by Mr. Brown and others at the foot of the Lake. So it became necessary either to pay damages and let Mr. Brown retain his land, or to expropriate the land and cause the Crown to become the owner. If 163J
I remember rightly-my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior will tell me if I am wrong-something like 1,200 acres of land owned by Mr. Brown were expropriated. Am I right in that?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
That is approximately
correct.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
So that there would be 700 acres of land in addition to the 500 which had been bought some years before from the department ait $1 per acre. I was Minister of Public Works at the time this expropriation took place, and I thought that it would be very much better to expropriate the land and secure an eiftire title to it than simply to pay damages and allow Mr. Brown to- continue in ownership. In this way, the Crown could better go on with the improvements. We did expropriate the land, and it will be remembered that we took not only that land owned by Mr. Brown which at certain times, even before the dam was built, was flooded with water, but also the dry land, the best part of his farm; we took both good land and bad. The Exchequer Court valued the whole 1,200 acres at this price of $25 an acre, so that while he was getting an average price of $25 an acre a good deal of the land of which he had been the owner before he bought the land from the Crown was worth perhaps three times as much as the land which at certain seasons was covered with water. More than that, the ^expropriation of the land meant the breaking up of Mr. Brown's ranch and farming enterprise, because the taking away of 1,200 acres of his land would necessitate his farming elsewhere. Unless, therefore, one knows all these facts, one can hardly say either that the judge of the Exchequer Court allowed too much, or that Mr. Brown paid too little some years before for that portion of the expropriated land which had been covered with water. It has been stated -and no one ought to know this better than my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior -that land which in 1900 and in 1902 was not worth more than $1.50 or $2.50 an acre, even before 1907 had risen to $15, $20, $25 and, in some cases, even $40 an acre. A great advance in the price of land took place, because the people had begun to come in. No matter how good the land is, there will be no increase in value until there is an bicrease in population, because it is popu-.ation that makes a demand for and increases the value of the land.
I should like to say just a word in reference to the Edmonton Bulletin. The eon

missioner, Mr. Ferguson, the Minister of the Interior, and the Solicitor General went far afield to make a charge against the Minister of the Inferior when they dwelt at length upon the fact that in 1905 the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company took stock in the Edmonton Bulletin. One would think, to hear these gentlemen talk, that this is the first great railway company that ever took stock in a newspaper. I remember when the late Peter Mitchell, formerly a member of this House and one of the most honourable gentlemen in this country-a gentleman who, as my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries knows, stood very high in the estimation of the people of New Brunswick and who occupied a very influential position in the government of the country-was editor of.the Montreal Herald. The Montreal Heralld was supposed to be owned by one of the railway companies of Canada, a company which has during all the years of its corporate existence, had to do with the different governments of the day. All railway companies, as hon. gentlemen know, have business to do with the different governments of the day. All railway companies, as hon. gentlemen know, have business with the Government and with Parliament. But no one ever suspected for one single moment that Mr. Mitchell was thereby influenced or induced to show any favouritism .towards that railway. I happen to know that in New _ Brunswick not long ago a railway company took stock in a new.spaper. The .fact became public; no doubt the same thing has been done privately on many occasions. So far as I am concerned, I never supposed that that circumstance would influence the proprietor of the newspaper in the way of extending any favouritism to the railway. What was the condition at the time the Grand Trunk Pacific Bailway Company took this stock? The contract had been entered into in 1903,and the amending contract in 1904. So far as those interested in the newspaper might assume, the contractual relations between the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and the Government of Canada were fixed and settled. It might have been different if at the time that the company were before the Government in connection with entering into the contract, they went to the proprietor of any paper who was a member of Parliament or a member of the 'Government and made a suggestion as to what they would do if their project were supported. But in this case nothing of that kind occurred; everything was settled. One can very well

understand that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company would take stock in the Edmonton Bulletin without the slightest idea that that would cause them to be entitled to any favour from the member for Edmonton.
Mr. SAM. SHARPE: The contract was modified in 1906.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
Yes, but the modification was of the very slightest character; it was one which was not in contemplation in 1905. Hon. gentlemen may 11 p.m. ask, as the Minister of the Interior did ask, why the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company took stock in the Edmonton Bulletin. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company was interested more than any other company in the development of the northern country, and in the development of the city of Edmonton. Is it not a well-known fact that real estate men establish newspapers at their own expense for the purpose of advertising the country in which they are interested ? The more rapidly Edmonton was built up and the more widely its resources became known-.and they could not be made known in a better way than through the medium of a strong, energetic newspaper published in the city- the better it would be for the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. One can well understand that the enterprising manager of that company would be well disposed to encourage the existence and the successful carrying on of a newspaper in a city in which they were so deeply interested. If hon. gentlemen want to be suspicious, of course they can conjure up some sinister motive on the part of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Compatiy, but I think it cannot be said either that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company intended to influence the hon. member for Edmonton or that there is the slightest ground for suspicion that the hon. member for Edmonton ever was influenced by the fact of their having taken .stock in the Edmonton Bulletin.
The hon. Solicitor General says that as a matter of fact the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company did get favours from the late Government. I venture to say that there never was an instance in which the Government drove so hard a bargain with a railway company as it made with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company at that time. How different it was from the contract made by the Conservative Government with the Canadian Pacific Railway!

Hon. gentlemen know what concessions were made, I will not go into them; but witth the Grand Trunk Pacific there was not an acre . of land given, not an acre of land which they could sell to settlers, not an acre of land which they could divide up into city, town or village lots, not one. In that respect they were treated in a manner wholly different from that in which the Canadian Pacific railway were treated. They were compelled to pay, by way of rental, interest on the entire cost of the road after the expiration of seven years from the time of construction. I say that was a hard bargain which the Government made with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company; and never afterwards did they show any disposition to treat that company in any very lenient manner, simply doing justice to them, holding them to their bargain. Again, my hon. friend says: Why they came later on and they got $5,000,000 which they had deposited with the Government, in exchange for bonds of an American railway company. Now that is a specious statement for the Solicitor General to make-if you are to allow your imagination to lead you into drawing conclusions from a statement which really contains nothing. The Solicitor General does not say that these securities were worthless; he does not say that they were not interestbearing securities; he does not say that they were not worth par; he does not say that they were not just as good as gold, or as bank notes; and yet, without giving you or this House the slightest information as to the value of those securities, :he would rather lead you to believe that some great favour was given to the company because an exchange was made. Take the insurance companies doing, business in Canada, they are required to put up security but they are not compelled to put up gold; they are allowed to put up securities in the way of bonds, Canadian, American or British, so long as they have a market value equal to the amount of the security which they are required to give.
Now, with regard to the Alberta Land Company. I must confess that I am not able to follow the commissioner or the Minister of the Interior in the suggestion that the department was guilty of wrongdoing in connection with the Alberta Land Company. The fact is that that company, according to his own admission, have expended $6,000,000 upon the enterprise in which they are engaged; and that very soon they will have that undertaking completed
and will have so completed an enterprise which both Governments recognize will be of an enormous importance to the country. Then what is there to complain of? My hon. friend in some portions of his speech says that concessions were given to a company that did not put up any money; but he complains of the concession to that company because they have put up the enormous sum of $6,000,000 and have carried out their undertaking almost to a succesful conclusion, and he says that because of the hard times, because of their not being able to go on with their own means and complete the undertaking this Government have returned to them the sum of $150,000 in order to encourage them to,complete this most worthy, most meritorious enterprise. That is the effect of what my hon. friend says. I would like to know, under those circumstances, what there is to complain of so far as the action of the department is concerned.
It seems to me to be another evidence of the fact that this Mr. Ferguson felt he had to earn his $40,000 in some way or other and that, if he could not find any good ground on which to condemn the late Administration, he must report upon matters in regard to which there was very little to complain of, hoping, I suppose, that the Minister of the Interior and those associated with him would take the bulk of his report in lieu of the quality and by reason of the many thousands of pages which he could obtain they would be satisfied, would never take the trouble to read it through and would pay him accordingly. A reference has been made to a lease of grazing lands in connection with the Blood Indian reserve. This House should always bear in mind that there is no allegation that the association of individuals who got that grazing lease did not pay all that the land was worth. There is no suggestion of that kind, there is no suggestion that it was leased by the department to them for one dollar less than it was fairly worth. The whole allegation is that the department turned down a gentleman, -whose name I have forgotten for the moment, and gave the lease to a Mr. McEwan. They say that Mr. McEwan represented a gentleman in Toronto, Mr. Peter Ryan, whom I have always heard spoken of as a very worthy gentleman indeed.
Mr. SAM. SHARPE: Pretty tricky.
Mr. PL1GSLEY:	Have he and the hon.
gentleman ever hunted together?

Mr. SAM. SHARPE:	He was an auctioneer.	.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
I have known some very respectable auctioneers. He occupies the very responsible position of registrar of deeds in Toronto. I have always understood that he is a gentleman of high character and he has been registrar for something like 25 years occupying the position under both Governments and it remains yet for somebody to make a charge that he has ever failed to perform his duties in a manner entirely satisfactory to the public. It is said that Mr. Ryan gave a one-sixth interest in this grazing lease to a Mr. Jones, and that Mr. Jones held it in trust for Mr. Pedley. That may be so or it may not; but this must be borne in mind, that the commissioner, Mr. Ferguson, as I remember reading the report-I do not confess to have been able to read it very carefully as I did not see it until this afternoon

but as I remember from my cursory reading, the commissioner does not say that he has any evidence which would show that up to the time of granting the lease to Mr. McEwan there was anything irregular or that the matter was carried on except in a straightforward way-not the slightest evidence which would justify him finding that and he does not find it. This is a fact which will not be disputed that, according to Mr. Ryan's evidence, Mr. Pedley had of late years been assisting him a good deal financially. Mr. Pedley had been endorsing his notes, he had been accepting his drafts and, as I remember his evidence, he said that years ago when Mr. Pedley was poor and he was better off he used to assist Mr. Pedley, but in later years the obligations had been entirely the other way, Mr. Pedley had been assisting him. And I would judge from the evidence that Mr. Ryan, having got this grazing lease, thought that he would put one-sixth of it in the hands of Mr. Jones as security for the meeting of his obligations to Mr. Pedley. That does not appear to have been communicated to Mr. Pedley at the time. The commissioner does not intimate anything of the kind and it is not entirely unreasonable that Mr. Ryan had done it in that way. At all events, we must be fair to a gentleman who has been charged with wrong-doing and, in the absence of evidence, we have a right to assume that he was innocent of any wrong-doing.
That appears to be the transaction. Later on, when the property was sold, Mr. Jones, who had had transactions also with

Mr. Pedley, sent him the sum of $900. Mr. Pedley thought apparently that that was a return of moneys which Mr. Jones was owing to him in connection with other transactions. Afterwards they got together and both agreed that this would be the proceeds of the sale of this one-sixth interest. Mr. Pedley swears that when these obligations of Mr. Ryan, in connection with these notes and drafts, are taken up this money will all belong to Mr. Ryan. This is not a very important matter, but it does not appear that Mr. Pedley had any knowledge whatever that Mr. Ryan was holding this one-sixth share until long after Mr. Pedley could be of any further assistance as far as the lessee was concerned.	.
There are some other matters referred to with which I do not intend to take up the time of the House. But before passing away from this subject I want to say that Mr. Pedley's conduct came to the knowledge of Mr. Sifton who was then Minister of the Interior. Are hon. gentlemen going to declare before this House that they are of the opinion that Mr. Sifton would allow dis-. honesty in his department? I have heard pretty nearly every hon. gentleman here praise up Mr. Sifton to the skies.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: No, not always.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
Not always, but of late years. I have seen the most eulogistic statements made in the newspapers of the Conservative party in regard to Mr. Sifton, and M.r. Sifton is a gentleman whom hon. gentlemen were 'apparently proud to follow in the fall of 1911. I know Mr. Sifton. I know him to be an honourable man, and when this was brought to his attention by a gentleman who had been a competitor for this lease, I do not believe that Mr. Sifton would so fail in his duty as to allow it to go uninvestigated at the time. I believe he did look into it and came to the conclusion that there was no wrong-doing on the part of Mr. Pedley. He continued Mr. Pedley in the responsible position which he was then occupying in the department.
I pass over this and come to a matter which perhaps might better be left to the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) himself to answer. I would leave iit to him of course, with full confidence' that he would be able to answer to the satisfaction of this House. But my hon. friend is suffering from a cold, and he might not want to go into these matters'to-night. Hon. gentlemen know how much affected his throat is. I would feel it my duty just to make

a reference to it in view of the Statements which have been made by the Minister of the Interior and in view of the 'letter which he read to this House. What is the allegation there? It is that a Mr. Fahrni had purchased some 3,000 acres of 'land in the Michel Indian reserve in 1906, that after that gentleman had made his first payment of something like $5,000 for the lanu he had not been able to pay any more. Apparently he was not able to get people to put their capital into it because he was not able to raise any more money and he was in danger of losing the property. The suggestion of the minister is that the department at Ottawa, from some 'sinister motive, notified Mr. Fahrni that they would cancel the agreement for the sale of the property, forfeit the money which had been paid and resume ownership and possession of the property. Then it is stated that subsequently, by reason of Mr. Anderson, who was a son-inrlaw of Mr. Oliver, interesting himself in the matter and desiring to make the purchase, the fact that the department had cancelled the sale might be taken as evidence that they were bringing pressure for an illegal purpose upon Mr. Fahrni so as to enable Mr. Anderson to obtain the property at a very much less amount than its fair value. I think I have stated fairly what is the suggestion of the offence as made by the Minister of the Interior. If that were the design one would think the Department of the Interior would have continued in existence the cancellation of the agreement for sale until Mr. Anderson had consummated the deal and made the purchase. All the evidence is right to the contrary. The evidence is that the department rescinded the order of cancellation and rescinded it before Mr. Anderson had made the purchase. It appears from the letter which the hon. Minister of the Interior had read that when Mr. Fahrni sold to Mr. Anderson he had the notice from the department that the order of cancellation had been rescinded. Therefore, he was quite free to hold his land knowing that the department would wait on him for his next payment. Let me read the letter:
X need not go into all the details as, as I have already stated, you are without douht familiar with same, but the letter which was written by your department, .notifying my father of cancellation for the sale of land had the desired effect on my father, and after receiving same he was prepared to do anything, in order to save whatever possible of the money which he had paid down.
Just at this stage, your son-in-law's enquiries came to hand, and naturally we were
ready to clutch at anything which would he of advantage to us, and we were prepared to sell at a sacrifice if necessary, provided we could give title. As soon as the question of our ability to give title arose, along came the notice from your department, dated June 7th 1910, in which you re-instate our contracts; thus malting it possible for us to put a legitimate deal through and your son-in-law, through fraud and mis-representation with the connivance of the Department of Interior, succeeded in obtaining the lands at about one quarter of their real value.
What does that show? It shows that after Mr. Fahrni had got notice from the department that the agreement was cancelled by reason of his failure to pay, Mr. Anderson got into communication with him and he said that he could not deal with Mr. Anderson, but that fortunately there came notice from the department that the order of cancellation had been rescinded. He does not pretend that he had come to any agreement with Mr. Anderson before that. He certainly had made no sale to him before that, but the fact of his getting notice from the department left him free to make an agreement with Mr. Anderson, and it placed him in a position in which he could give title. Is not that an extraordinary thing if the department were desiring to force Mr. Fahrni to sell his property at a sacrifice? Is it not remarkable that if through the desire of the department, before any binding agreement had been made, or any agreement at all had been made, between Mt. Fahimi 'and Mr. Anderson, they should rescind the order of cancellation and so in effect notify Mr. Fahrni that there was no necessity for him to sacrifice the property, but that the department would wait upon him for the payment which was then due.
I do not know what the property was worth. One complaint of the Minister of the Interior seems to be that a great injustice has been done because the $5,000 that Mr. Fahrni had paid had not been forfeited and gone into the Treasury of this country. The Minister of the Interior talks about these different transactions in which he says great losses occurred, but let me tell him that if he puts all these together they would not in the whole amount to the value of that land at Prince Albert which was sold to Mr. Donaldson by the Department of the Interior after this Government came into office, for the magnificent sum of ten dollars. All put together would not amount to what was taken out of the Treasury of this country in that one land transaction, and yet the Minister of the Interior bemoans the fact that some $5,000 which

Mr. Fahrni had paid to the Government was not forfeited, but that Mr. Fahrni was allowed to get his $5,000 back.
There is another remarkable fact about this letter, and one which is worthy the attention of members of this House. This is a copy of a letter which was sent, not to the Minister of the Interior, but to Mr. Frank Oliver, M.P., and a copy of it evidently has been sent to the Minister of the .Interior, in order that it might be used in this House on this motion. This precious letter is dated Gladstone, March 9, 1915, and I shall quote one statement from it:
It appears most conclusive to me that we have been defrauded out of some $50,000, which I have no doubt can be obtained by carrying the matter to a civil court, and it further seems to me that a perpetrator of a crime of this kind would also be criminally liable. What I ask and what I must insist on having is some restitution of this damage, and unless the same is made immediately all the documents shall be handed over to my solicitor for his attention.
When I used to be practising law, the writer of a letter like that was called a blackmailer, and I have always understood that a gentleman who accepts a copy of a letter like that and endeavours to use it for the purpose of intimidating the person to whom it is addressed, becomes associated in that attempt at blackmail.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: Oh!

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
I have always understood that to be the law. Let me read that portion of the letter again:
It appears most conclusive to me that we have been defrauded out of some $50,000, which I have no doubt can be obtained by carrying the matter to a civil court, and it further seems to me that a perpetrator of a crime of this kind would also be criminally liable. What I ask and what I must insist on having is some restitution of this damage, and unless the same is made immediately all the documents shall be handed over to my solicitor for his attention.
And I suppose his solicitor has been handed a copy of this letter as well as all the documents, and the solicitor has handed them over to the Minister of the Interior. I do not know anything about what the writer of this letter states, but I am inclined to think that some degree of credit will have to be given to my hon. friend, that he has resisted this attempt at blackmail, and that he has in effect said to this man: If you have any claim against me, either civil or. criminal, go ahead and take the matter into the courts whether you wish to resort to civil or criminal proceedings; you have no claim against me,

no shadow of conspiracy can be substantiated against me, I will not be compelled by your threats to accede to your demands, go and do your worst. That is in effect what my hon. friend from Edmonton has said. And because evidence of wrong-doing has been made apparent to my hon. friend from Edmonton, as it has been made apparent to the people of this country, and because frauds have been committed in the purchase of war supplies, my hon. friend felt it his duty to denounce the wrong-doing, it has remained for the Minister of the Interior to lend himself to the efforts of this blackmailer who attempts to asperse the character of the hon. member for Edmonton.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this very laJte hour I do not propose to trespass for any considerable time upon the patience of the House. It has been .my privilege to be intimately acquainted with the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) ever since I went to western Canada, now some seventeen years ago, and I say in all sincerity that because of my relations with him, which were always friendly, I hesitate to discuss this report in the sense in which I otherwise would. It is not always pleasing to find that a public man in whom you have placed confidence is not worthy of the confidence you have reposed in him. It is not always pleasing to find that a public man whom you believed to be a man of integrity and probity is the opposite. It is not always pleasing to believe that those who have been charged with the administration of departments of the Government, have been unworthy of the confidence that has been placed in them and have been derelict to their duty. And, Sir, for those reasons, more in sorrow than in anger, I direct attention for a few moments to-night to the report which has been laid on the table of the House. I cannot but conceive this to be the end of the public career of the hon. member for Edmonton, as it should be the end of the public carrer of the hon. member for As-siniboia (Mr. Turriff).
I should like to say to this House as one coming from western Canada, that those who live in eastern Canada have very little understanding of what has taken place in (that country during the past fifteen or sixteen years. There are very few public men in eastern Canada who have taken the trouble to study the conditions under which we have lived; the conditions under which we were per-

mitted to exist by the Government led by the right hon. the leader of the Opposition. During the fifteen years that Government was in power, what did they do? They were not content with taking the fishes in the takes and granting fishing monopolies to their friends, but they took the waters in the streams which give life to the parched and arid lands of the plains and they handed these waters out to their friends to monopolize and to prevent their use by the poor. Not only this, but the timber and the trees of the forest they handed out to favourites, and to-day honest men in the Senate, whom we heard referred to the other day, are timber licensees throughout western Canada. Does my hon. friend say that if you cannot find the name of Tom Davis among these licensees you will not find the name of some other equally reprehensible senator? If you cannot find the name of a senator who has a timber lease or a water-power, you will find the name of one who has a lease of coal lands, which by some method he wrung out of the reluctant Minister of the Interior of that day. And, not content with exhausting the fish and the waters, and the timber and the coal, they had a scheme for getting the other mineral resources under the surface of the earth. The coal lands were gone, and when they were gone they issued grazing leases to their friends, their brothers-in-law, their uncles-in-law, their sons-in-law, and every other relation they could possibly conceive of. When you cannot get a son-in-law, you get some one else who will -answer just as well and when you cannot get a brother or e cousin or -an aunt, you get -some one relates in some way or other, -and you hand him or her part of the public domain. During the fifteen years from 1896 to 1911 everything that could be done to alienate the public resources of Canada by conspiracy on the part of the hon. gentlemen who then were administering the country and -their -friends, was done. There is not time to-night to go into all the details, because it would take hours to do it; but I live in the province of Alberta, and I sa,w men with nothing, grow suddenly rich at the expense of the public. I saw the land of this country being alienated-graft is the proper word to describe the situation-by men whose corrupt ideas degenerated -and degraded the public life of Ith-e country; and when an election came around, we found them acting as the camp-followers of the then Minister of the Interior. They were
the porch-climbers and the thugs to whom he referred; they were the men who in 1905 and 1913 robbed and opened the ballot boxes of Alberta; they were the men who interfered with the -sanctity of the ballot, and who did not permit the people of the province to express th-ei-r will -at the polls. I presume- my hon. friend referred to them this afternoon when he spoke of porch-climbers and thugs, for they wer-e the porch-climbers and thugs, and I engaged the time of a detective agency for two years until I traced to its source the opening and robbing of the ballot boxes by these men. I suffered from their work, because I was chosen by the electorate of -the city of Calgary, and the ballots of the constituency were opened and the ballots abstracted and I was counted out. But o-ne would think that it would be sufficient that -all these things should have happened, but it was not. Lo, the poor Indians they must suffer ! The wards of the nation! The aborigines of Cahada! The men whose rights they were sworn to protect were the victims of the conspiracy of a Turriff, a Ped-ley and -a White. If anything has ever in the annals of Parliament been placed upon the table of -this House calculated to bring the blush of shame to the face of any Canadian, it is the revelation contained in the evidence that is here to-niarht.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
I would like to correct
my hon. friend; I was never connected in any shape, form or manner, directly or indirectly, with the Indian Department.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman who has just spoken is quite correct as to not being associated with Mr. Smart and Mr. Pedley and Mr. White. He chose his brother-in-law, Mr. Adamson, as his associate.
As if that were not sufficient, my hon. friends opposite had to proceed to corrupt public opinion. One would think, Sir, that after having exhausted every known means by which to exploit the public domain to the limit, the fishes in the sea, the heavens above the earth, and the water under it, my hon. friends opposite would have been content. No, public opinion must be corrupted with a subsidized press. The bon. member for Edmonton, in Ms own person, stood here to-day, as the proprietor nominally and as the editor in fact, of a Grit journal that existed by the money of a great transportation and public service company for the purpose of corrupting public opinion. These are the indictments which this report makes against these gentlemen-conspiracy, fraud, dereliction of duty, breach of trust, and, above all,

a deliberate attempt and intent to destroy and corrupt public opinion. What, Sir, happened in Alberta? At the very time that the hon. gentleman from Edmonton was negotiating a little deal with Mr. Frank Scott of the Grand Trunk Pacific, at the very moment that he was inducing him by honeyed words to put $15,000 into his great journal, that great fireside journal, his henchmen had charge of the campaign in which the ballot boxes were robbed. If any man is curious to-night to know in what manner public opinion was dealt with during those days, let him go to the Parliamentary Library and read the Edmonton	Bulletin	of	those	days.	Ah, Sir,I am a personal sufferer; I have been the	victim	of	the	$15,000 filched
from this public service company; I have been the subject of the attacks of these hired assassins; I know whereof I speak, and I speak feelingly. The people of the province in which I live suspected that these men had not suddenly grown so wealthy that they had thousands of dollars to cast about the streets in maintaining this gang of camp followers who went to the polls throughout the province; we did not believe that they had suddenly found the wealth in the soil and dug it out and spread it around in this way; but little did the confiding electorate of Alberta believe that the great stalwart, sturdy, determined, outspoken, grimly honest man, as he said, had sold for $15,000 the independence of the press. What will they say when they find that these attacks that have been made upon the public men in the province in which I live, who do not see eye to eye with some hon. gentlemen opposite, were being paid for by a great railway company? When the hon. gentleman the other day in such measured tones deprecated the passing of the legislation that we were about to pass dealing with the Grand Trunk Pacific, when he expressed the great fear that he did that vested interests would be interfered with, that the credit of the Grand Trunk Pacific might be affected, little did we think that $15,000 of the money of that very company was speaking.
Ah, Sir, it is indeed a sad spectacle. A long career- of great usefulness to his friends and himself is about ended. I have stood as chairman of a great public gathering and introduced on a Dominion Day my hon. friend the member for Edmonton as a citizen of whom we might well -be proud; I have pointed out those sterling qualities that have made for him a great 
place in the state; I have pointed out those qualities of heart and mind that he had from the day when he crossed from Winnipeg to Edmonton until he sat here as a minister of the Crown, little dreaming that such a report as this would indicate how little warranted was my confidence in him. I speak the thoughts of the many thousands of the province of Alberta who to-morrow morning will read my words; when they understand that this their one time idol has feet of clay, when they find that those feet of clay are firmly embedded around about the Bonaventure station in Montreal; and when they realize just exactly what his obligation and duty are to the Grand Trunk, they will say: " Our idol has fallen." It was only fitting that the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition should have entertained the same opinion, for to-night he deserted his one-time colleague and friend. Ah, well, my hon. friend from Edmonton after all was the heir to some of these things about which we have spoken to-day, and he did not create-nay, he only had to carry out. When one contemplates that, one might think that he would say with Wolsey:
, " Had I but served my God with half the zeal
I served my King, he would not in mine age,
Have left me naked to my enemies."
If he were not so disposed to think in the words of Shakespeare, he might have thought in the words of the Psalmist:
" If it were an enemy that had done me this dishonour, I could have borne it; but it was thou, even thou, my own familiar friend. We took sweet counsel together."
Deserted in the house of his friends, flung to the dogs, forgotten, remembered no more. The right hon. gentleman who led the Government for fifteen years; and had him as his colleague for six, speaks no word of commendation, no word of defence, no word of. recognition of the sterling qualities that endeared him so to the people of the West. Gone, forgotten, remembered no more! Peace be with him! And so he passes from the public life of Canada, forgotten, I take it, for his leader has forgotten him, remembered no more except for the wrong he has done and the legacy of evil he has left with us.
And now whom do we pass on to? We pass on to the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff). And who, contemplating that noble form in our public life, can fail to feel the force of the observations he made touching the public service of Canada? Who can fail to remember his

observations touching the British preference and other matters? Think of the way in which he discharged his duties as land commissioner, and his noble thoughts for all those friends of his who are remembered now not as common men, but as huge colossi, I suppose, who look down upon us poor common mortals. Millionaires! some are knights, and some are about to pass out into dark night forever. Let us deal with him. Why, when first I came into this House and ventured to raise my voice here, the first words I heard snarled across the House, were " C.P.R." Think of' the hardihood of the man capable of doing that. And he talked about " unholy hands " the other evening, and called upon high Heaven to be witness to his honesty, his integrity, his nobility of character, his splendid fervour for the public weal. And did he think then of the Brown lease? Sir, some man we know not who, some hand we know not whose, between the time a certain document passed into the hands of the hon. member for Assiniboia with "32" written upon it changed that to "60" and it never went out of the clutches of the hon. member for Assiniboia. I should like-indeed, I should like -to deal with many of these matters at length.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: Go on.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
But I am not going to, because the hour is late. I want to make a few observations only touching the Department of the' Interior in connection with one or two of the matters which have been mentioned here to-day. The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) has endeavoured to-night to support the position of his friend from Edmonton. With that sense of loyalty in which he is not lacking and which did not distinguish his sometime leader, he rallied his splendid talents to the support of his friend from Edmonton. But the woeful cry almost from the beginning indicated to us that it was not a congenial task; it was a work too great even for his master-mind.
There is one matter about which especially I desire to speak-the Brown grazing lease. What are the facts? A man named MacGregor, a beneficiary of the system came down to Ottawa and happened to run across a man named Brown. He said: " If I want a lease perhaps you will let me use your name. I have all the area I can hold in my own name." "Certainly," was the answer, "Ido not mind a little thing like that; I live down in Montana." The application was put in. The hon. member for Assiniboia was
Commissioner of Dominion Lands. MacGregor looked the thing over and did not think much of it. A man named Bell thought he would like to look into it. Later it transpired that a gentleman named Adamson thought it would be a good thing to get hold of. Mr. Adamson happens to be a close relative of the hon. member for Assiniboia. One good turn deserves another. Brown had sent in an application for
32,000	acres of land under a closed lease- arid a closed lease in the terminology of the department, meant a lease that might be subject to cancellation after two years' notice,-and, under the control of the gentleman who now sits in this House and talks of " unholy hands," there came out an irrevocable lease for 60,000 acres.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
I do not know whether
the hon. gentleman wishes to be fair orgiot, but he must know that that lease was issued a year and a half after I left the department.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, certainly that is so. The hon. gentleman realizes as he told us the other night, how poorly paid the civil servants were, and he too was in that case when he left the Civil Service; he was still poor on the occasion of his leaving the Civil Service. He left behind him this memorandum, that an application for a closed lease for 32,000 acres should become an irrevocable lease for 60,000 acres. And it was his handiwork and nobody else's. It is idle to try to get away from that. I have the evidence. He was summoned and gave evidence before the commissioner and explained exactly what happened.	That
evidence is too long to read.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext: Read it.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF MR. T. R. FERGUSON.
speechtext:
No, it would take too long to read that evidence to-night. Hon. members themselves can see the bulk of it. He was not, as some one has said, taken unawares; he was confronted . with the facts and given an opportunity to explain them; and his evidence as to how it happened is upon that record. It will be printed; it will be read by the people of Canada; but there is only one explanation the people of Canada can gain from it, and that is that anxiety to assist a brother-in-law brought about the change from 32,000 acres to 60,000 acres. That is the fact and no glossing over, no sophistry, no endeavour to get away from the real facts, can disguise this-that there was alienated

in the province in which I live a most valuable tract of land, one that should have settlers upon it. To satisfy the avarice and greed of a brother-in-law,
60,000	acres of the best land in that province was alienated on an application that went into the hands of the hon. member for Assiniboia as an application for 32,000 acres. And the lease is irrevocable, though the application was for a closed lease. I say that there is no explanation that can be given to the people of this country that can change the opinion in the province I come from that this was a deliberate act on the part of this machine to take from the people for the benefit of political favourites a part of the great resources that should be held in trust for the people and not for one or two political heelers and partisans. Why, Sir, there is only one person who benefited by the increase in that acreage, and that is Mr. A. J. Adamson, who was then after the lease. He concealed his connection with it from the department until July, 1905, when he sent to the department a quit-claim deed from this same man, Brown, to the Galway Horse and Cattle Company-which was Adamson, under another name, and enclosed a cheque for $650 for rental. Thousands of dollars of rental were left uncollected, for the rental was not paid between the date of the granting of the application and the issue of the lease in 1905. And the man whose handiwork this is, is the man who goes through the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta supporting the party of hon. gentlemen opposite and who dares to come into this Parliament and talk about "unholy hands." There may be travesties of justice, arid there may be things that bring the blush of shame to Canadians, but what disgusts most men in Canada is the rank and arrant hypocrisy of some of our public men. The evidence is that this deed, which was brought to the department in 1905, was dated September, 1903; the name of the person to whom it was assigned was left blank, and this was afterwards filled in. Then what happened? The Galway Horse and Cattle Company was not in existence at the time of the assignment, nor was it in existence for some time afterwards. It was a company which was formed by Adamson for the purpose of holding this tract: that is embodied in the evidence that he himself gave. They allotted to the members of this little company their shares, and when Mr. Turriff-not as the hon.- member for Assiniboia, but as the former Commissioner of Dominion Lands-testifying before the com-
missioner, was asked upon his oath to explain how the change respecting the increase in the area had been made, he could offer no explanation whatever. There is no doubt that he did it for Adamson, and Adamson, having decided not to go into the ranching business, turned the lease over for $22,500 to John Cowdry. All that it had cost Adamson for rental was $650; this he paid in July, 1905. The report showed that he should have paid $2,400 more for arrears of rental at that time, and that the department allowed the lease to be issued without demanding the money which should have been collected as rental-they practically made a present of $2,400 to Adamson and his company. I ask the hon. member for Edmonton, I ask the right hon. leader of the Opposition, whose supporters these gentlemen are: can any excuse be given to the people of the province of Alberta-Brown swears that he made no application and did not know that the lease had been changed until he gave his evidence before the commissioner-why that closed lease was changed to an irrevocable lease of 60,000 acres while the transaction was under the control of the now hon. member for Assiniboia? You may offer excuses; you may trifle with the truth; you may endeavour to palliate the effect, but there it stands, in all its grim reality. It was but one instance of the working of a system from which the people of western Canada suffered for fifteen years. I do not present that single instance as standing alone. The instances multiply; the illustrations increase. They are not isolated; they are not one here and another there; they are a continued, considered, persistent series of illustrations and instances showing a deliberate conspiracy on the part of a few men to enrich themselves at the expense of the people of that day and of the posterity that was to be. It was a deliberate attempt on the part of those men to filch from the settlers and from the settlers that were to come the public domain of the province of Alberta and to hold it until they could turn it over at a profit, as speculators and exploiters, to the loss of the people of Canada.
When you couple that single illustration, of which I have given the details, with the others that are dealt with in the report, and remember that iln that province there is no voters' list-nothing but a system of enumerators worked by political partisans before the election-when you keep that fact in mind, together with the observations made

by the hon. Solicitor General, I ask, what elections have we had in Alberta or in Saskatchewan during the last fifteen years? The party press rejoices, and in flaring headlines holds up to the public the story that the Liberals won in Alberta and Saskatchewan; but I say that there has not been an election in. either of the two provinces, since they became provinces, that is worthy of the name of an election. There has not been conducted under the auspices of the Conservative party in these western provinces a single election since 1896-and the population of those provinces was then but a few thousands, a handful of people. AH the new settlers who came from across the line and from foreign lands across the seas have been brought into Canada and taught the damnable doctrine that public men holding high offices are there to corrupt, not always with dollars, but oft times with the natural resources of the country: a coal lease here, a fishing permit there; an irrigation right here, a quarter-section there. Then, when that failed, if the poor, untutored Indian happened to have a few acres of land, he was not free from the avarice and the greed of these Shylocks of out land. Is it any wonder that public opinion is outraged? Is it any wonder that the public conscience is aroused? Is it any wonder that when men went through the country
12 p.m. and spoke to the people from the public platform, they said: "these people are right at heart"; yet when the votes were counted on election day, the results were quite different? The right hon. gentleman who leads the Government went through western Canada and found a sound sentiment and a splendid response to the principles that he enunciated, but when the votes were counted, his candidates were always in the minority. Why? Ask Cruise and Davis and Turriff and Adamson and Oliver and Marshall, and that gang of freebooting buccaneers who went round the country as campaign followers of the then Administration. These are strong words, but these are the words which the dictionary says describe the men that I mention, and I know of no other language which I can use to do justice to the occasion.
This Aylwin tract affair is one of the most despicable transactions that was ever endeavoured to be put through in this country. I want to be fair to the hon. member for Edmonton. He protested as long as a man could, but finally, as compromise is the price of all government, he yielded, and
to-night he pays the price of his yielding to his friends in the Cabinet. The Aylwin tract lies east of Calgary. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company several years ago was carrying on large irrigation works in that locality.
Suddenly there appeared one McGregor. I would like to traverse his history this evening and tell this House of that long and devious trail that leads from Brandon to the Yukon and from the Yukon to Medicine Hat and along through the Southern Alberta Land Company and then back to Brandon again; but I have not time. Suffice it to say that having conceived the idea that where water would flow down hill there might be a chance of making some money by using it on the arid lands of the province, he organized a company. It is a sad story. If I had time to tell of the English investors who paid 40 shillings in the pound for their shares that have gone to six shillings ! I know of widows in England who put money in the South Alberta Land Company's stock. I know of the absolutely untrue statements contained in the prospectus, and how that money was obtained. I know of the sanction given by the late Government to the operations of the company. My hon. friend from Edmonton was not then minister, let us be fair. But that reminds me that there was not only Mr. McGregor but several other gentlemen. One of them is now in the Senate, my friend Senator Ross, of Moosejaw; he was there and Hitchcock was there, another relation of somebody's else's relation, and these men foregathered and conceived the idea of the company. They obtained certain concessions. [DOT] They purchased certain cattle. The Grand Forks Cattle Company turned in its property. It is too long to tell about tonight, but they got their company and when Aylwin and his friends saw the splendid exploitations made by this company in London, when they saw the way in which the English investor caught at the bait held out about this irrigable land and what fortunes there were to be gathered from it, they said:	This is not
right, we want some too. You know there is nothing equal to the avarice that a transaction like that sometimes creates in human nature, and so Mr. Aylwin looked about and said:	There is 350,000 acres of
land not far from this tract in southern Alberta, and if we can get some water from the river for irrigation there is a fortune in it. So they came down to my friend from Edmonton; and on the 1st of August, 1906, he wrote a letter in which he said:

This is a very important matter. . . The question is one of engineering, which must bo very definitely settled, especially as the area involved is considerable. You may rest assured there will be no loss of time in arriving at a conclusion in regard to it.	[DOT]
That was a proper course to take, the course you and I would expect any reasonable minister to take. He said that as it was a serious matter it required to be carefully considered. But that was not sufficient for Mr. Aylwin for I find on the 21st of September, 1906-mark you that the first letter was on August 1, and on the 21st day of September of the same year, when my friend the Minister of the Interior returned from a little trip to England, there was placed before him a memorandum by the then and now Deputy Minister of the Interior which will, I trust, direct the attention of the right hon. gentleman to the ignoble part he played in connection with this undertaking:
Ottawa, September 21, 1906. Hon. Frank Oliver,
Minister of the Interior.
Memorandum.-I beg to submit herewith the papers in connection with the application of Mr. Aylwin for a tract of land in connection with his' irrigation scheme. As per the terms of your letter to Mr. Piche, Sir Wilfrid instructed me to have Mr. Stewart make the inspection therein mentioned; his report is attached.
Peradventure there may be another Sir Wilfrid rather than our own right hon. gentleman, but at least his name and fame are not known to the Canadian people.
The memorandum continues:
On the receipt of Mr. Stewart's report the matter was again submitted to Sir Wilfrid, and he desired me to state to you that in his opinion the application should be dealt with in the same manner as the Robins' application, and that he would have granted it and passed the necessary Order in Council but for the fact that you were then on the ocean on your way home. On that account he thought it better to let the matter stand until your return, for the necessary action.
So that these gentlemen, having retained the services of a then Liberal member of Parliament, Mr. Pichei, to act as their solicitor, after the hon. the Minister of the Interior of that day had instructed the engineer to make a report, during his absence had taken the matter up with the right hon. gentleman who was then the Prime Minister and Acting Minister of the Interior and he was prepared to grant that application, according to the statement made by the Deputy Minister of the .Interior. But that is not all. I observe that these gentlemen found, when the hon. member for

Edmonton came home, that he was not quite the easy man to deal with they thought he would be, because he said: I do not quite see it that way. He conceived the idea that he would not tie up those 350,000 acres for these people and he did something else-He said: " I am going to throw some of this land open to homesteaders "-and he did it. Mark you the determination of the hon. member for Edmonton; mark you the noble patriot desiring to assert and protect the rights of the people; for a year he did it. A whole year had gone by and the thing had not been put through. Behold this illuminating epistle from Mr. Robert of Montreal regarding this action of the hon. member for Edmonton:
Montreal, March 18, 1908.
H. A. Aylwin, Esq.,
Winnipeg.
My dear Aylwin,-Your telegram to hand, and in answer would say that I understand that Oliver has thrown tract open to homesteaders, but other than being evidence that Oliver has not been straight in the matter, I would not let it worry you unduly, as the matter is in such shape that they cannot but grant it, and will have to give you a tract of similar size, and I am satisfied that from my last interview the matter will be granted this session.
I am going up to see Sir Wilfrid in a day or so, and trust to have some good news for you on my return.
Keep your friends quiet until you hear from me, and I am as certain as ever that you will get your grant of land. The delay has been very annoying and disgusting, but they are in a worse position to refuse it to-day than tbey were a year ago.
I trust Mr. Newton is keeping better; give him my kind regard.
I remain,
Yours truly,

That was in March, 1908. The general election was approaching; always, with stealthy tread, nearer and nearer it came, and, peradventure, far be it from me to suggest it, Mr. Robert may have been a prospective campaign contributor. Far be it from me to suggest it, but what followed? The hon. member for Edmonton, with that sturdy independence which characterized him on an occasion which perhaps he has forgotten, was still determined that he would not even then hand the tract over to these men, and so for a year he stood out. Mr. Robert felt confident of what he could do; he had only to see Sir Wilfrid. And so we find this letter, on the 27th of July, 1908, a few months later-the election was approaching nearer:
Dear Sir,-Yours of the 24th to hand, and in reply would say that I have no objection to

meeting Hudson, but rather think our best course would be to keep ourselves as free as possible until we get matters straightened with the Government.
I am supposed to have my interview with Sir Wilfrid next week to finish up matters, and will let you know the result as soon as possible.
With kind regards.
This is the gentleman whom the right hon. gentleman hardly knows.
His brother.
What about the system?

The system had not
been working well just then. Mr. Robert wrote the following letter:
September 21, 1908.
I am in receipt of yours of 8th, but owing to my absence I did not get it till my return from Ottawa, and I intended writing you at once, but had to leave town unexpectedly the next morning, and only just returned.
I was unaware that Mr. Newton was on the note concerning deposit with Government.
I do not want to .put up the money at present moment for this deposit, especially as the money lies at our credit in hands of Government and your Bank has transfer for same.
Then he discusses what is to be done:
On my last trip to Ottawa, I had the whole matter approved and accepted, and the order is on the table, signed by minister, and has approval of Government, and will be signed by Government and Governor General before November 1st.
Notice, about November 1. This is September. Why delay? Far be it from me to
say what the reason was. October 26 was the fateful day and of course this waits until the 1st November. Then he says:
We have made note due November 24th to enable the whole matter to be finished, so that we will, I hope, be able to make a part division before that date.
The spoils of war!
I have spent a considerable sum already on this, and have assured its successful completion within a few weeks, and do not, under the circumstances, think it out of my way to ask you to put this through, when I give your Bank another name on note as good, or possibly better than the one they have now, and trust you will arrange matter.
This suggested a change in the name of one of the endorsers and gave the name of [DOT] Westgate, who was said to be worth a quarter of a million instead of the name of somebody else. Mr. Robert said that he wanted eighteen cents an acre for his influence. I do not know what that word ''influence" means. There is evidence that this term indicates an ability on the part of some gentleman to get very close to the ministers of past days and induce them to do certain things regardless of the public interest and the public weal. Influence and prices seem to have a fixed relation to each other. If the price of land is good the price of influence iis high, if the price of land is low influence is cheap. If the lands of the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Valley Company -are only worth $1.25 an acre the price of influence is away down, but if on the other hand, the price of land goes up then the price of influence goes u.p too. I do not know what influence was worth in the market at that time, but I know that in this case the influence of Mr. Robert was being sold at eighteen cents an acre and that they divided the spoils.
Cast lots?

No, they did not cast lots. They should have cast lots as to which should have gone out even as one in ancient times went out and made away with himself. What happened? As soon as these gentlemen got this land they incorporated a company called the Alberta Land Company, not the South Alberta Land Company. Robert and his associates then made an effort to hold up McGregor. It must have been a novel sensation for him. They went to him and said: We have this land. Oh, yes, says McGregor, but do you not know that I was ahead of you, that I saw the Minister of the Interior and I got all the water. You have the land and no water; what'-are you going to do about it? The minister had handed

these people out a lemon in the shape of land with no water on it. What a sardonic smile he must have had on his face when he sold them this land without any water! What happened? Alexander Smith, of Ottawa, now appears on the scene. I know this House has never heard of that little transaction which he put through. McGregor found the money to buy up the Alberta Land company, the result of which was that the 69,000 acres passed into the hands of the South Alberta Land Company. They had the water and they got the land. The right hon. leader of the Government seems to have been very anxious to put this proposition through, but in the absence of the Minister of the Interior he thought he had better wait until he came back. When he came back he found him very reluctant, very obdurate. He was, to use the words of an hon. member of this House, a bucking broncho from the West who, .when driven to make possible the sale of this land by his Prime Minister, handed out this lemon in the shape of the land without the water.
There was another transaction in my country in connection with the Kanana-kis coal deal, in which there figured not only the names of Howard Douglas, two sons and his son-in-law, but two or three government officials. One of them never heard of the fact that he had ever been a great landed proprietor till the investigation. He merely signed his name, he did not know that anybody else signed his name in his absence, but as a result there passed out of the hands of the Crown a very valuable coal property that has since been sold for $500,000. There is another case not far from my own country in connection with the Blood Indian reserve which has been touched upon. Then they talk about these conspiring and culpable officials being dismissed. If there is one thing more than another that should convince this House that the Government of this country cannot be carried on by a Conservative Government with men of this stamp occupying administrative positions it is the evidence that was given by Pedley, by White and by Smart. I do not want to traverse the ground gone over to-night by my hon. friend the Solicitor General, but if ever there was a self-convicted perjurer, it is Frank Pedley. If there ever was a man who admitted that he had perjured himself in the endeavour to steal a few dollars, if there ever was a man who was a self-confessed perjurer and a criminal unfit for the public service of Canada, it is Frank Pedley. It is time for us to revise our ideas about this matter. L say as a supporter of the Government

that they have been entirely too lenient with civil servants who have prostituted their positions. I say that all the wrongs we have had in this country, all the offences that have occurred since the defeat of the Liberal party have been the result, not of the actions of this Government nor of tne ministers who compose this Government, but of the men who were occupying positions in the public service when this Government came into power and who have given evidence of the training which they had in former days. How can you expect men to be loyal to the public service who have been recreant to their trust in days gone by? You have the cases of Pedley, Smart and White. Smart has now left the service, but White is kept there against my protest. How can you expect a man of that type to discharge the duties and functions of his office when he has been recreant to the trust reposed in him by the people and the Government of the day? These men have admitted that they have committed acts which stamp them as being unfit for the public service; if men such as they are going to have the sympathy and support of hon. gentlemen opposite, what must the people of Canada think of them? I have heard men stand up here and take hours talking about dismissals from the public service, 'but no wonder the public service is rotten if you have hon. members opposite standing up and vindicating the position taken by a Pedley, or a White or a Smart. This thing must stop, and this report will enable it to be stopped. I cannot continue longer, for ' the. hour is late.
Go on.

I am not making a speech about this; I only rose to make a few superficial observations. This all may sound to some hon. gentlemen to be a very light thing, but it is not. It strikes at the very root and foundation of our institutions. I do say, Mr. Speaker, in all seriousness, that I have endeavoured during the time I have lived in western Canada to play my small part in the public life of that country, and I have been disappointed, as many men have been, by reason of the various results in elections. I have taken the trouble to ascertain the reason why. I have seen men of integrity-at least, I thought them so- and of worth, and of character, succumb to the powerful influences, to the tremendous pressure that can be exercised upon them by reason of the facts to which I have directed attention. I appeal to the right hon. gentleman opposite, with his

forty-one years of parliamentary experience, to at least stand in his place, before this matter ends, and make a declaration that will make for the integrity and for the uplifting of the public life of Canada. I at least hope that as a resuH of these unfortunate revelations, and they cannot be less than matters of great sorrow arid sadness to most men, good may come. Do you mean to say to me	that a matteT	of this kindwhich strikes at the very existence of the body politic, is lightly to be passed over? You laugh when the member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) endeavours to do something to protect the poor red man, and you laugh because the red man's heritage is taken from him on the Blood reserve or somewhere else, and we talk about the glories of our democracy and the freedom of our franchise, but if men occupying high public places are permitted, with the approval of their leader, to go back to the electorate and ask for their support after they have been shown to be guilty of acts so nefarious, so dishonourable, so destructive to the morale of the community and so degrading to the national life, then there is absolutely no hope for democracy or for the proper development of Canada. I appeal to men, to whom, after all, love of country is greater than love of party, to read those reports as they are published. They are not partisan reports, they are not violent attacks upon men, or individuals, but a plain laying open to the perusal of the people of Canada of chapters in its national life that are degrading to that life, and humiliating to every man who calls himself a Canadian. That is the reason I ventured to speak in general terms of all these things dealt with in the report, and to direct specific attention to only one, or two, or three of them.
