We know what the hon. gentleman from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) pointed out with his camera in days gone by as to what took place with timber limits, and we know he was laughed to scorn. Why, Sir, look at the timber limits of western Canada and the men who own them. Go study""the men; study these different coteries who got these limits by a system that could only be operated with the connivance of the officials, and that is so clear and so palpable that it does not require proof. Why, some of these men have the hardihood to appeal to the electorate, and some of them fold their arms smugly and say: What have you to say about it; we have the support of the people behind us. I do not often tell stories, but I	will	tell this
one. Once in western Canada a man was charged with stealing a pig, and the evidence was clear, and a verdict of guilty seemed inevitable, but to the surprise of the judge and counsel, the jury filed into court and pronounced him not guilty. And when the prisoner was discharged his counsel said to him: "How do you account for this verdict?" and the late prisoner replied: "Say, that's easy, don't you know that each man of the jury had a piece of that pork?" And, Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) comes back and talks of the magnificent majorities he has got in times past,
I refer his electorate to the story of the Riding Mountain, the alienation of the public domain, which took place in his time, and then I think how the men who had a bite of the pork can be competent to judge between him and the best interests of this country. I would like to, and I shall do it later, review the evidence in these cases from my own provinces. I am content to place myself on record as regretting, perhaps more than I can say- although it may be of benefit and advantage to the party I support in this Parliament-my feeling of real sorrow and very great regret that these things should have happened in the province in which I live.
I hopefully look to it, in fact I almost believe, that the right hon. the leader of the Opposition, notwithstanding his connection with some who are guilty, will before this Parliament prorogues, in his place, give to the people of Canada some encouragement or some word that will indicate that regretting as he does the past he looks forward to a brighter future, although he has no hope or expectation of ever being in a position to duplicate the past.

Mr. Speaker, I would claim the privilege of answering the personal references made by the Minister of the Interior, but I regret that my voice will not enable me to do so, and for that reason I shall not ask the privilege of the House. As the matter related to two departments, I brought in a recommendation to Council myself that a commission should be issued and a gentleman named for the purpose of inquiring fully into all the matters which had been alleged. The inquiry has now been completed, and I desire leave to lay upon the table of the House the evidence that was taken upon the inquiry and the report of the commissioner.
Motion for the adjournment of the House (Mr. Oliver) negatived.

Mr. SPEAKER read a communication from the Governor General's secretary, announcing that His Royal Highness would proceed to the Senate Chamber on Thursday, the 15th April, at 4 p.m., for the purpose of proroguing the present session of Parliament.

speechtext:
May I, with the consent of the House, lay on the table the report of Mr. R. A. Pringle, K.C., commissioner appointed to inquire into certain matters connected with the construction of drill halls at Orono, Meaford, Blackstock, Markdale, and other places in the province of Ontario. Information came to me some two or three months ago dbarging that certain irregularities and certain frauds had been committed in respect to these drill halls, some of winch were under construction by the Department of Militia and some by the Department of Public Works.
Sir ROBERT BORDEN moved the adjournment of the House.
